sections.title: Three problems, one machine
sections.body:
An operating system is not a program you run. It is the program that runs everything else, and it exists because the bare machine is a hostile place to put more than one program. That machine offers one CPU that executes one instruction stream, one flat array of physical memory that any instruction may address, and storage that keeps only what was deliberately written to it. Everything the OS does answers one of three problems that follow from those facts.

**Virtualisation** is the first and the largest. The OS takes one physical resource and presents many virtual ones: a virtual CPU for every process, so ten programs each behave as though they had the machine; a private address space for every process, so each may believe its memory starts at zero. None of this is free - every virtual thing costs bookkeeping, and the machine spends real time maintaining the fiction rather than doing your work.

**Concurrency** is the problem virtualisation creates. Once many things run at once and can be interrupted between any two instructions, sequences that look indivisible are not: a counter increment is a load, an add and a store, and another process may run in the gaps. The OS suffers this worse than anyone, because it is itself a concurrent program handling interrupts from devices that do not wait to be asked.

**Persistence** is the third, and it is different in kind. Memory forgets everything when power goes; a file system must not. That means the OS has to write data in an order that survives a crash halfway through, which is why writes are buffered for speed and then forced with `fsync` for safety - and why a program that never forces its writes can report success on data that is not yet anywhere durable.

annotations.text: Nothing in this program mentions the other copies, checks a schedule, or yields. The illusion is complete precisely because the program contains no code to maintain it - that work is entirely the kernel's.

`sleep` is where the process gives the CPU up, which is why four copies interleave neatly. Remove it and they still interleave, but only because a timer interrupt takes the CPU away from each in turn - and that is the more interesting case.

checkpoint.prompt: For each operating system feature, name which of the three problems it exists to solve. Answer with exactly one of `virtualisation`, `concurrency` or `persistence`.

steps.label: each process gets a private address space starting at zero
a lock protects a counter shared between two threads
a journal entry is written before the file system is updated
one CPU is time-sliced between ten running programs

checkpoint.explain: Virtualisation is always the same shape - one physical resource made to look like many - so both the address space and the time slice belong to it. Concurrency is the problem that appears only because virtualisation succeeded: things now overlap. Persistence stands apart because it is not about sharing at all, but about surviving the loss of power, and the tempting mistake is to file the journal under concurrency because it also involves ordering.

sections.title: The process, and the three states it lives in
sections.body:
A **program** is inert: bytes on a disk describing instructions and initial data. A **process** is that program plus everything the machine needs to keep it going, and the OS's central abstraction is exactly the list of what that turns out to be.

There are three parts and they are worth memorising, because the list is not arbitrary - it is precisely what must be saved and restored so that a stopped process cannot tell it was ever stopped. First, its **address space**: the memory it can address, holding code, static data, a heap that grows one way and a stack that grows the other. Second, its **registers**: the general-purpose registers, and especially the program counter, which says which instruction is next, and the stack pointer, which says where its frames are. Third, its **open files**, the descriptors it may read and write, with 0, 1 and 2 conventionally standard input, output and error. The kernel keeps all of this in a **process control block**, one per process, and switching between processes is little more than saving one such record and restoring another.

A process is at any moment in one of three states. **Running** means it is on a CPU executing instructions. **Ready** means it could run and the scheduler has simply not chosen it. **Blocked** means it cannot use a CPU even if offered one, because it is waiting for something else - a disk read, a key press, a child to exit.

Only four transitions exist, and the two that do not exist teach more than the ones that do. Ready to running is **scheduled**; running to ready is **descheduled**; running to blocked happens when the process itself initiates a wait; blocked to ready happens when the awaited event completes. There is no ready-to-blocked edge, because a process must be running to ask to wait, and no blocked-to-running edge, because the scheduler picks only from the ready set. Blocked exists as a separate state for exactly one reason: a process waiting on a disk would otherwise be chosen over and over to accomplish nothing.

annotations.text: The program counter and stack pointer are the two registers that make the abstraction work: together they say which instruction is next and where the local variables are, so restoring them resumes a process mid-expression without its knowledge.
Open files belong to the process, not to the program. This is why a shell can redirect a command's output by changing the descriptor before the program it is about to run even exists.

checkpoint.prompt: One process is created and runs to completion. Give its state immediately after each event. Answer with exactly one of `ready`, `running`, `blocked` or `done`.

steps.label: the kernel has created it but not yet scheduled it
the scheduler has just picked it
it calls read() on a file not in the cache
the disk interrupt reports the data has arrived

checkpoint.explain: The fourth step is the one people get wrong: an I/O completion makes a process runnable, not running. The interrupt handler moves it into the ready set and returns; whether it gets a CPU next is the scheduler's decision and may be some time away. Answering `running` there collapses the ready state entirely, and with it the whole distinction between being able to run and actually running.

sections.title: fork, exec and wait - and why they are three calls
sections.body:
Unix creates processes with a call that is strange the first time you meet it. `fork()` makes a near-copy of the calling process - its own address space, its own copy of the descriptors - and then **returns twice**: in the child it returns 0, and in the parent it returns the child's process id. The child does not start at `main`; it continues from the same point in the same code, which is why the return value is the only thing distinguishing the two copies.

`exec()` does something no other call does: it replaces the current process's image with a different program. Same process id, same open descriptors, but new code, new heap and a fresh stack. It does not return on success - there is nothing left to return to, because the code that called it has been overwritten.

`wait()` blocks the parent until one of its children exits, and collects the exit status. A child that has exited but not yet been waited for is a **zombie**: nearly all of it is gone, but the kernel keeps its status because someone may still ask for it.

Why is creating a process not one call? Because the gap between `fork` and `exec` is where all the interesting work happens. In that gap the child is running the parent's code with the child's identity, and it can rearrange its environment before the new program exists to have an opinion about it. Redirection is the classic case: the child closes descriptor 1 and opens a file, which takes slot 1 because `open` returns the lowest free descriptor - and then `exec`s a program that writes to standard output knowing nothing about any of this. A single combined `spawn` call would have to accept every possible adjustment as an argument. The cost of the design is a full address-space copy that is usually discarded microseconds later, which is why real systems implement `fork` with copy-on-write rather than by copying anything at all.

annotations.text: The whole trick of shell redirection. Descriptor 1 was just closed, so it is the lowest free number, so `open` returns it - and the file quietly becomes standard output for whatever runs next.
This line runs only on failure. On success there is no code left to return to, because `execvp` has overwritten the very instructions that called it.

checkpoint.prompt: A program contains `fork(); fork(); printf("A\n");` and nothing else. Give the counts asked for, as plain integers.

steps.label: processes in existence after the first fork returns
processes in existence after the second fork returns
lines of A printed in total
lines printed if a third fork is added before the printf

checkpoint.explain: Each `fork` doubles the population, because every process reaching that line - parent and previously created children alike - splits in two, so $n$ forks in sequence leave $2^n$ processes. The common wrong answer of 3 comes from imagining the parent forking twice while the first child does nothing; but the child continues from the same point in the same code, so it meets the second `fork` too.

sections.title: Two modes and the one door between them
sections.body:
If a user program could execute any instruction, there would be no operating system worth the name: it could reprogram the interrupt table, disable the timer and never give the CPU back, or read another process's memory by rewriting the page table. So the hardware carries a **mode bit**. In **user mode**, privileged instructions - direct device I/O, changing the page table root, disabling interrupts - do not merely misbehave, they raise an exception. In **kernel mode**, everything is permitted.

The obvious question is how a process ever gets service, given that it cannot do the privileged things itself. Not by calling kernel code: a plain jump to a kernel address would run that code with the caller's privilege, which protects nothing at all. Instead it executes a **trap** instruction. The hardware saves the caller's registers onto a **kernel stack**, raises the privilege level, and jumps - and this is the essential part - to an address the kernel chose at boot and installed in a **trap table**, never to an address the user supplied. The user program says **which service** it wants by putting a system-call number in a register; it does not and cannot say **where** to go. Returning is the mirror image: a return-from-trap instruction restores the saved registers and lowers the privilege level in one step, and the process resumes at the instruction after the trap, no wiser.

So the **system call** is the only door between the two worlds, and the kernel owns both its position and its lock. `open`, `read`, `write`, `fork`, `exec` and `exit` are not library functions in any interesting sense; each is a thin wrapper around a trap.

That door is expensive to walk through - a mode switch, register saves, and a cold effect on caches and the TLB - which is why libraries buffer. Writing one mebibyte in 512-byte chunks means 2048 `write` calls; routing the same bytes through a 4 KiB buffer means 256. Eight times fewer crossings for identical output, and that ratio is the entire reason `printf` sits in front of `write`.

annotations.text: One instruction, and the machine is in kernel mode executing code the kernel published. Note what is absent: no address of any kernel function appears here, because the caller is never permitted to name one.
The system-call number is how a user program chooses a service. It is an index the kernel validates, not a pointer it trusts - which is the difference between a controlled door and an open one.

checkpoint.prompt: Complete the two halves of the kernel boundary.
checkpoint.template:
regs.rax = SYS_write;    /* say which service is wanted */
___;                     /* the instruction that raises the privilege level */

/* the hardware jumps to an address installed at boot in the
   ___ table, and never to an address supplied by the caller */
checkpoint.explain: The two blanks are the two halves of the guarantee. The trap instruction is what changes the mode - a program cannot set the mode bit directly, or the bit would protect nothing - and the trap table is what fixes the destination, so the caller chooses a service by number but never chooses an address. Remove either half and user code could enter the kernel wherever it liked, in kernel mode.

guided-practice.prompt: You type `./prog` at the shell. Put the steps the operating system takes into the order they must happen, ending with the program's first instruction.
fragments: read the program's code and static data from disk
allocate an address space and load the code and data into it
allocate a stack and place the arguments to main on it
allocate a heap region for later growth
open descriptors 0, 1 and 2 for standard input, output and error
set the program counter to the entry point and enter the process
guided-practice.explain: The order follows from the definition of a process: everything in its machine state must exist before its first instruction runs, because that instruction may immediately push a frame, call `malloc` or write to standard output. Setting the program counter is necessarily last - it is the moment the inert program becomes a running process, and nothing can be prepared after it.

guided-practice.prompt: For each transition, say whether it is possible for a process. Answer `yes` or `no`.
guided-practice.explain: The two impossible edges follow from who performs the transition. A blocked process cannot go straight to running because only the scheduler grants a CPU and it chooses from the ready set - so an I/O completion makes a process runnable, never running. And a ready process cannot become blocked, because blocking is something a process does to itself by executing a call, and a ready process is executing nothing at all.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete the parent-and-child skeleton so that the child replaces itself with a new program and the parent waits for it.
guided-practice.explain: `fork` returns 0 only in the child, so that comparison is the sole way two identical copies tell themselves apart - testing for a positive value would select the parent's branch instead. `execvp` overwrites this process's image rather than starting a new process, and `wait` is what keeps the parent from racing ahead and from leaving a zombie behind.

guided-practice.prompt: A colleague argues that virtualisation is pure overhead: the machine has one CPU and a fixed amount of memory whichever way you slice it, so pretending otherwise can only cost time. Explain what the pretence buys that justifies the cost, and name a concrete cost it imposes.
guided-practice.explain: The colleague is right about the resources and wrong about the goal. Virtualisation is not trying to create CPU cycles; it is trying to make one machine usable by many programs each written as though alone, and to stop any one of them reading or corrupting another - protection and transparency, not throughput. It also raises utilisation rather than lowering it: while one process is blocked on a disk its virtual CPU costs nothing and a real one runs somebody else, which a single-program machine simply cannot do. The costs are real and worth naming honestly - saving and restoring machine state on every context switch, kernel memory for a control block per process, and a scheduling decision the hardware would otherwise never have to make.

process-tracing.prompt: Two processes share one CPU. The scheduler runs a process until it blocks or exits, and prefers P0 when both are ready at the start. P0 needs 4 ticks of CPU, then a disk read taking 3 ticks, then 2 more ticks, then exits. P1 needs 5 ticks of CPU and no I/O. Give the state of **P0** during each tick listed, using `running`, `ready` or `blocked`.
process-tracing.explain: P0 uses ticks 1 to 4, then blocks for the disk over ticks 5, 6 and 7, and the completion at the end of tick 7 makes it ready - not running. Ticks 8 and 9 are the point of the exercise: P1 already holds the CPU and this scheduler does not take it away, so a process perfectly able to run waits two more ticks for a reason that has nothing to do with it. Reading `ready` as `running` there compresses the run to nine ticks and hides the queueing delay entirely; it really takes eleven, of which P0 spends six running, three blocked and two merely waiting its turn.

process-tracing.prompt: Consider `fork(); printf("X\n"); fork(); printf("Y\n");` with no other statements and no `wait`. Give each count as a plain integer.

steps.label: processes running when the first printf executes
lines of X printed in total
processes in existence after the second fork
lines of Y printed in total

process-tracing.explain: The two forks do not have the same effect, because the printfs sit between them. Two processes reach the first `printf`, so X appears twice; both then fork, so four processes reach the second and Y appears four times, for six lines rather than eight. The trap is doubling everything at the end - but the X lines were printed while the population was still two, and nothing reprints them. Note also that the six lines may appear in any order, since no `wait` imposes one.

process-tracing.prompt: A process with pid 3720 calls `int rc = fork();` and the new child is given pid 3721. Both then run `printf("rc=%d pid=%d\n", rc, (int)getpid());`. Give the value each expression has in each process, as a plain integer.
process-tracing.explain: One call, two returns, and the asymmetry is deliberate: the parent is told which child it made, because it will need that pid to wait for it, while the child needs no such information and receives 0 - a value no real pid ever takes, so the test is unambiguous. The tempting error is to expect the child's `rc` to be its own pid, which would leave the two copies genuinely indistinguishable and the whole idiom unusable.

process-tracing.prompt: The kernel is about to switch the CPU from process A to process B. For each item, say whether it must be saved as part of A's machine state before the switch. Answer `yes` or `no`.

steps.label: A's table of open file descriptors

process-tracing.explain: The rule is not 'everything belonging to A' but 'everything B is about to overwrite'. Registers are the scarce shared thing - there is one set of them and B is about to use it - so they must be copied out. A's heap and its descriptor table are already private per-process structures that B never touches, so they simply stay where they are; copying them would make a context switch cost time proportional to the size of the address space, which is exactly what the design avoids. The page table root is a register too, which is why it sits on the yes side while the memory it describes does not.

process-tracing.prompt: A build script forks a child to compile a source file, and the parent immediately proceeds to link the resulting object file. It works on a fast machine and fails intermittently on a loaded one, complaining that the object file is missing or truncated. The child's compile command is correct. What is the cause?
process-tracing.answer: the parent never calls wait, so it runs concurrently with the child instead of after it
process-tracing.explain: `fork` returns in the parent as soon as the child exists, not when it finishes, so without `wait` the two run concurrently and the linker may open the object file while the compiler is still writing it - or before it exists at all. The intermittency is the signature: on an idle machine the child usually finishes inside the parent's own startup work, and on a loaded one the scheduler simply does not give it that head start. The fix is `wait(&status)` before linking, which both imposes the ordering and yields the exit status, so a failed compile is not silently linked against.

kernel-boundary.prompt: Put the steps of a single system call into the order the machine performs them, from the kernel's preparation to the user program's resumption.
fragments: at boot, in kernel mode, the kernel installs the trap table
the user program places a system-call number in a register
the user program executes the trap instruction
the hardware saves the caller's registers onto the kernel stack and raises the privilege level
the hardware jumps to the handler address recorded in the trap table
the kernel validates the call number and performs the service
return-from-trap restores the saved registers and lowers the privilege level
the user program continues at the instruction after the trap
kernel-boundary.explain: Two of these orderings carry the whole security argument. The trap table is installed at boot, while only the kernel is running, so by the time any user program exists the destinations are already fixed and cannot be nominated by the caller. And the privilege is raised by the same hardware step that transfers control, not by an instruction the program could issue on its own - if a program could raise its own privilege and then jump, the mode bit would protect nothing.

kernel-boundary.prompt: A developer moving from a bare-metal embedded board to Linux ports a driver routine that writes a byte straight to a device register with an `out` instruction at a fixed I/O address. Compiled and run as an ordinary user program, it dies immediately, with no output at all, and the device is never touched. What is the cause?
kernel-boundary.answer: the process is in user mode, so the privileged I/O instruction raises an exception and the kernel kills it
kernel-boundary.explain: On the bare-metal board the code was the only thing running and was therefore effectively in kernel mode; under an operating system it is an ordinary process with the mode bit clear, and direct device I/O is precisely one of the instructions that mode bit forbids. The hardware raises an exception, control goes to the kernel, and the kernel kills the process - which is why the death is immediate and the device untouched, rather than the device being written and something failing afterwards. The port has to go through the door: reach the device through a system call on a device file, or move the routine into a kernel module that legitimately runs in kernel mode.

kernel-boundary.prompt: A logging library calls `write` once per log line, each line about 512 bytes, and produces one mebibyte of logs per minute. Profiling shows the process spending a surprising fraction of its time in the kernel. Explain why the number of calls matters rather than the number of bytes, work out how many `write` calls per minute it makes now and how many it would make through a 4 KiB user-space buffer, and state honestly what the buffering costs when the machine crashes.
kernel-boundary.explain: A mebibyte is 1048576 bytes, so 512-byte writes cost $1048576 / 512 = 2048$ traps a minute, while a 4 KiB buffer holds eight lines and reduces that to $1048576 / 4096 = 256$ - eight times fewer crossings for byte-for-byte identical output. Each crossing costs a mode switch, a register save and restore, and a cold effect on caches and the TLB, which is why the time appears in the kernel rather than in the logging code. The honest cost is on the other side: with buffering, up to eight lines the application believes it has written are sitting in user memory and vanish in a crash, and even after `write` returns the data is only in the kernel's page cache. Only `fsync` forces it to the device, and it is slow precisely because it cannot be batched - which is the trade every logger must make deliberately rather than by accident.

kernel-boundary.prompt: You are writing the section of a small kernel's design document that justifies the user/kernel split to a sceptical reviewer who wants user programs to call kernel routines directly for speed. Argue the design. State what the mode bit forbids and why each forbidden thing would otherwise defeat the OS; explain why a plain jump to a kernel address is not an acceptable substitute for a trap; describe what the trap instruction does that the caller cannot do for itself, including where the destination comes from and when it was decided; and account for the cost of a crossing and how libraries reduce the number of them. There are no tests here: your answer is marked against a rubric of the points it must cover.
kernel-boundary.hint: Work outwards from the reviewer's proposal and ask what it would let a malicious program do. Each answer to that question is one of the privileged instructions, and each privileged instruction is one of the OS's guarantees.
kernel-boundary.explain: The argument has a shape worth learning. Each privileged instruction maps to a guarantee: disabling interrupts would let a program keep the CPU for ever and destroy the virtual CPU; changing the page table root would let it read any process's memory and destroy the private address space; direct device I/O would let it bypass the file system's permissions entirely. The reviewer's direct call fails not because of where it goes but because of what it does not do - it does not change the mode, so the kernel code runs unprivileged and faults; and if it did change the mode, then any address in the kernel could be entered at any offset, including the middle of a routine just past the point where it checked its arguments. The trap answers both: in one uninterruptible step it saves the caller's registers on a kernel stack the user cannot reach, raises the privilege level, and transfers to a handler recorded in a table the kernel installed at boot, so the caller selects a service by number and never nominates an address. The cost is real - a mode switch, register saves, cache and TLB effects - and the right response is not to widen the door but to walk through it less often, which is exactly what a buffered `printf` in front of `write` is for: one mebibyte in 512-byte pieces is 2048 crossings, and through a 4 KiB buffer only 256.

exam.prompt: What does it mean to say an operating system **virtualises** a resource?
choices: It presents one physical resource as many virtual ones, each easier to use than the whole
It simulates the hardware in software so that programs need not be compiled for the machine
It moves the resource from hardware into a file so that it survives a reboot
It hides the resource entirely so that no program may use it
exam.explain: Virtualisation is a transformation, not an emulation: one CPU becomes a virtual CPU per process, one physical memory becomes an address space per process. The tempting second choice describes an emulator or an interpreter, which is a different idea altogether - the instructions of a virtualised process run natively on the real CPU, and the illusion is about who owns the resource rather than what it is.

exam.prompt: Which of these are part of a process's machine state - the things that must be preserved so it can be stopped and resumed without noticing? Select all that apply.
choices: Its address space, holding code, static data, heap and stack
Its registers, including the program counter and stack pointer
Its open file descriptors
The scheduling policy the kernel uses to choose among processes
exam.explain: The first three are exactly the standard list, and the test for membership is whether resuming the process without the item would be detectable - lose the program counter and it cannot continue, lose a descriptor and its next `write` fails. The scheduling policy is a property of the kernel and is shared by every process, so it belongs to no one process's state; changing it alters when a process runs, never what it computes.

exam.prompt: Name the state a process is in for each description. Answer with exactly one of `running`, `ready` or `blocked`.

steps.label: executing instructions on a CPU right now
able to run, but the scheduler has chosen someone else
waiting for a disk read to complete
waiting for a child process to exit
just descheduled at the end of its time slice

exam.explain: The distinction that matters is between not running because nobody chose you and not running because you could not use a CPU if you were chosen. Waiting on a child is the same kind of waiting as waiting on a disk - the process asked to wait, and nothing it can do will make the wait shorter - so it is blocked, not ready, and the scheduler must not consider it at all until the child exits.

exam.prompt: A program runs `int rc = fork(); if (rc == 0) { fork(); } printf("Z\n");` and nothing else. Give each count as a plain integer.

steps.label: processes in existence after the first fork
processes that execute the inner fork
processes in existence when the printf runs
lines of Z printed in total

exam.explain: The guard changes everything. Only the child sees `rc == 0`, so only it forks again, and the population goes 1, 2, 3 rather than doubling to 4 - the original parent skips the inner call entirely. All three processes then reach the `printf`, which sits outside the `if`, so Z appears three times. Answering 4 is the reflex of counting forks instead of asking which processes reach them.

exam.prompt: Complete the shell's redirection idiom, run in the child between fork and exec.
exam.explain: Descriptor 1 has just been freed, so the lowest-free-descriptor rule hands it straight back to `open` and the file silently becomes standard output. The ordering is not stylistic: after `execvp` the code performing the redirection no longer exists, and the new program has no idea it was redirected - which is exactly the property that lets a shell redirect programs that know nothing about shells.

exam.prompt: Put the steps a shell takes to run `ls > out.txt` into the order they happen.
fragments: the shell calls fork, producing a child running the shell's own code
in the child, close descriptor 1
in the child, open out.txt, which takes descriptor 1
in the child, exec the ls program, replacing the shell's image
in the parent, wait for the child to exit
the shell prints its prompt again
exam.explain: Every redirection step sits in the gap between `fork` and `exec`, and that gap is the reason the two are separate calls at all: the child is the shell's code with the child's identity, free to rearrange descriptors before the program that will use them exists. Doing the `close` and `open` before the `fork` would redirect the shell itself, and doing them after the `exec` is impossible, because the code that would do it has been overwritten.

exam.prompt: Explain why the hardware, and not the operating system, must be the thing that enforces the user/kernel distinction - and what specifically the OS could no longer guarantee if the mode bit did not exist.
exam.explain: The OS is only software, and software cannot restrain software running on the same CPU: while a user program holds the CPU the kernel is not executing and can check nothing. Only the hardware is present on every instruction, so only the hardware can refuse one. Without the mode bit the two guarantees that define an OS both collapse - a program could disable the timer interrupt and keep the CPU for ever, destroying the virtual CPU, and it could load its own page table root or address devices directly, destroying isolation between address spaces and the file system's permissions with it. The mode bit is also what makes the trap meaningful, since a controlled entry point is only worth having when the uncontrolled ones are refused.

exam.prompt: A recorder writes 100 records of 512 bytes each with `fprintf`, through the default 4096-byte stdio buffer, and prints `saved` after the last one. The machine loses power immediately after `saved` appears. On reboot the file holds 96 complete records. Every record was formatted correctly. What is the cause, and why exactly 96?
exam.answer: the last four records were still in the user-space stdio buffer and had never reached the kernel or the device
exam.explain: Eight 512-byte records fill the 4096-byte buffer, so stdio issues a `write` only on every eighth record. One hundred records are 51200 bytes, which is twelve full buffers - 49152 bytes, or exactly 96 records - plus a remainder of four still sitting in user memory when the power went. Printing `saved` proves nothing: the program had merely finished calling `fprintf`. The deeper point is that flushing the buffer would only have moved those bytes into the kernel's page cache, which is also volatile, so durability needs `fflush` followed by `fsync` - and the reason nobody does that per record is the cost of the very crossing the buffer exists to avoid.

exam.prompt: Two processes each run the same loop incrementing a shared counter one thousand times. The final total is sometimes 2000, often less, and never more. Explain what concurrency problem this is, why virtualisation is what created it, and why the outcome varies between runs on the same machine with the same input.
exam.explain: An increment is not one action but three - load the counter, add one, store it back - and a process may be descheduled between any two instructions. If both load the same value before either stores, two increments produce one, so updates are lost and the total can only ever come out too low, never too high. Virtualisation created the problem directly: giving each process the illusion of its own CPU means the kernel takes the real one away at moments neither process chose, so the interleaving is decided by timer interrupts and scheduling decisions that differ from run to run. That is why the same program on the same input gives different answers - the nondeterminism is in the schedule, not in the code, which is exactly what makes such bugs so hard to reproduce.

sections.title: Direct execution, and the two things that go wrong
sections.body:
The previous floor gave every process the illusion of owning the machine. The obvious way to run one is **direct execution**: load the program into memory, jump to its first instruction and let it run on the real CPU. That is not merely the fast way, it is the only way that is fast - any scheme where the OS inspects each instruction before it runs costs orders of magnitude, which is why emulators are slow and real operating systems are not.

Direct execution alone gives the machine away, and it gives it away twice over. The first problem is **restricted operations**: a running process must be able to read a file or send a packet, yet it must not be able to read **any** file or scribble on the disk directly. The second is **regaining control**: once the OS has jumped into user code, the OS is not running any more, so how does it ever get the CPU back?

The answer to the first is the word **limited** in **limited direct execution**. The hardware carries a **mode bit**. In **user mode** the privileged instructions - issuing I/O, loading the page-table register, disabling interrupts - simply fault. In **kernel mode** everything is permitted. Crossing between them is not something a process may do at will; it happens by executing a **trap** instruction, which raises the privilege level and jumps **simultaneously**, to an address the process did not choose.

It did not choose it because at boot, in kernel mode, the OS installed a **trap table**: one entry per kind of trap, each holding the address of a handler. A system call is therefore not a call at all. The process puts a **system-call number** in a register - an index into a small fixed list of doors, not an address - traps, and the kernel decides what that number means. Let a process name the destination and the mode bit would be worth nothing, because user code could jump into the kernel wherever it pleased. On the way back the kernel executes **return-from-trap**, which restores the saved registers and drops the privilege level in one indivisible step.

annotations.text: Nothing here is checked, filtered or interpreted. This is the speed the whole design exists to preserve.
A number, not an address. The kernel maps it to a handler through the trap table, so the set of reachable entry points is fixed at boot.
One instruction that raises privilege and transfers control together. Splitting it in two would leave a window in which user code ran in kernel mode.

checkpoint.prompt: Complete the three terms. Write the first as a single word, the second as a single word, and the third exactly as `return-from-trap`.
checkpoint.template:
The CPU carries a ___ bit deciding whether privileged instructions are allowed.
User code reaches the kernel by executing a ___ instruction.
The kernel hands control back by executing ___.
checkpoint.explain: The mode bit is hardware state rather than something the OS keeps in a variable, because the check has to happen on every instruction without any software involvement. The trap raises privilege and jumps in the same indivisible step, and return-from-trap undoes both the same way - if either could be split, user code would briefly run privileged.

sections.title: Taking the CPU back, and handing it to someone else
sections.body:
The second problem is harder, because it is not obvious the OS has any lever at all. The **cooperative** approach is to wait: a process gives up the CPU whenever it makes a system call, and a well-behaved program is expected to call `yield` now and then. This works right up until a process contains an infinite loop that makes no system calls, at which point the only remaining remedy is to reboot the machine. That is not a scheduling policy, it is a hope.

The real answer is a **timer interrupt**. At boot, in kernel mode, the OS programs a hardware timer to raise an interrupt every few milliseconds. The interrupt is not a request the process can decline; the hardware stops it, saves enough state to resume it, and jumps to the handler the trap table names. The OS regains the CPU whether the process wanted to give it up or not, and that single fact is what makes pre-emptive scheduling possible at all.

Inside the handler the OS decides whether to keep running the current process or switch. If it switches, it performs a **context switch**, and the thing worth remembering is that register state is saved **twice**, by two different parties. The hardware, on taking the interrupt, pushed the running process's **user registers** onto that process's kernel stack. Then software - a short routine, usually assembly - saves the **kernel registers** of the outgoing process into its process structure and loads the incoming process's from its own.

The last register restored is the stack pointer, and switching it is the moment of the switch: from the next instruction onward the kernel is running on a different process's stack, so return-from-trap pops that process's user registers and resumes it exactly where it left off. None of this is free - a switch costs on the order of a microsecond in direct work, plus the far larger indirect cost of a cache and TLB now full of the wrong process's data - and that cost is what stops us slicing time arbitrarily finely.

annotations.text: Arming the timer is itself a privileged operation, and only the OS is ever in kernel mode at boot - so no process can disarm the thing that pre-empts it.
The first of the two saves. It is done by hardware, into the kernel stack of the process being interrupted, before any OS instruction runs.
The second save, done by software, into the process structures. Note the two arguments: one context is written, the other read.

checkpoint.prompt: Complete the account of a context switch caused by a timer interrupt. The last blank is a number written as a word.
checkpoint.template:
The ___ saves the running process's user registers onto its kernel stack.
Software then saves the outgoing process's kernel registers into its ___ structure.
Register state is therefore saved ___ times during one switch.
checkpoint.explain: The split exists because the two saves have different jobs: the hardware save happens before any OS code runs at all and preserves what the interrupted process was doing, while the software save preserves where the kernel itself was, so that the switch routine can be returned into later. Assuming a single save is the usual mistake, and it makes the stack-pointer swap look like magic instead of the pivot it is.

sections.title: Measuring a scheduler: turnaround and response
sections.body:
Now that the OS can take the CPU back, it must decide who gets it, and any such decision needs a number to be judged against. Two numbers matter and they are not the same. **Turnaround time** is $T_{completion} - T_{arrival}$ - how long the job took from the user's point of view, end to end. **Response time** is $T_{firstrun} - T_{arrival}$ - how long the job sat there before anything happened at all.

Start with **FIFO**: run jobs to completion in arrival order. It is trivially fair and it is fine when jobs are the same length. Give it three jobs arriving together, A needing 100 ms and B and C needing 10 ms each, and the turnaround times are 100, 110 and 120, averaging 110. The two short jobs waited a hundred milliseconds behind one long one for no reason except arrival order. This is the **convoy effect**, and you have met it at every supermarket till.

**Shortest Job First** runs the same three jobs shortest-first, and the average turnaround falls to 50. Nothing was made faster - the total work is identical and the machine did not change - only the order did, which is worth pausing on, because it means average turnaround is as much a property of the queue as of the hardware. SJF is provably optimal for turnaround when all jobs arrive together.

That last condition is doing all the work. Let A arrive at 0 needing 100 and let B and C arrive at 10 needing 10 each: SJF, being non-pre-emptive, is already committed to A, and the average turnaround climbs back to 103.33. **Shortest Time-to-Completion First** adds pre-emption - which the timer has just made possible - and re-decides whenever a job arrives, bringing the average back to 50. Both policies, though, need to know how long each job will run, and a real operating system does not.

annotations.text: A job can have an excellent response time and a dreadful turnaround time, or the reverse. Optimising one is not optimising the other.
The convoy: each 10 ms job carries roughly 100 ms of waiting that has nothing whatever to do with its own work.
110 down to 50 with no change to the machine. This is why scheduling is worth studying at all.

checkpoint.prompt: Three jobs arrive together at t = 0: A needs 100 ms, B needs 10 ms, C needs 10 ms. FIFO runs them in the order A, B, C. Give each turnaround time in milliseconds, and then the average.
checkpoint.explain: Because all three arrive at zero, each turnaround is simply its completion time, and completion times accumulate down the queue. B's 110 is ten milliseconds of its own work sitting behind a hundred milliseconds of A's - the convoy - and it is that inherited wait, not any inefficiency in B, that the average is reporting.

sections.title: Round robin, and a scheduler that learns
sections.body:
Neither FIFO nor SJF has any answer for an interactive user, because both run a job to completion before the next one starts. **Round robin** does the opposite: run each job for a fixed **time slice**, or quantum, then switch to the next. With three 5 ms jobs and a 1 ms quantum the average response time is 1 ms rather than SJF's 5 ms, and the terminal feels alive.

The price is exact and unavoidable. Those same three jobs now finish at 13, 14 and 15 for an average turnaround of 14, against SJF's 10, because round robin stretches every job across the whole run. Any policy that is fair in the short term is bad for turnaround: sharing the CPU evenly means nobody finishes early. Shrinking the quantum improves response and costs nothing on paper - but each slice ends in a context switch, so a quantum near the switch cost spends most of the machine on switching. The quantum is chosen to **amortise** that cost: long enough that the switch is a small fraction of the slice, short enough to stay responsive.

What we actually want is SJF's turnaround for the long jobs and round robin's response for the short ones, without being told in advance which is which. The **Multi-Level Feedback Queue** gets there by watching. It keeps several queues, each a priority level, and applies five rules. Rule 1: if A's priority exceeds B's, A runs. Rule 2: equal priorities round-robin between themselves. Rule 3: a new job enters at the **top** priority - an optimistic guess that it is short. Rule 4: once a job has used up its **allotment** of CPU time at a level, its priority drops one queue.

That is a scheduler that learns. A job that keeps consuming whole slices sinks and is treated as the long batch job it evidently is; a job that blocks for I/O after a millisecond never exhausts an allotment and stays near the top, getting excellent response. Two things then go wrong. Long jobs can **starve** if the upper queues never empty. And if rule 4 is written the naive way - as **give up the CPU before your slice ends and keep your priority** - a job can **game** it by issuing a needless I/O just before every slice expires, monopolising the top queue forever. Rule 5 fixes the first: every period $S$, move every job back to the top queue. Counting allotment as total CPU time used at a level, regardless of how many times the job relinquished the CPU, fixes the second.

annotations.text: Response improved fivefold and turnaround got forty per cent worse. The trade is not a quirk of this example; it is what short-term fairness costs.
`used` counts total CPU time consumed at this level. Counting completed slices instead is the bug that lets a job game the scheduler with a needless I/O.
The boost is the anti-starvation rule, and it also forgives a job that used to be CPU-bound and has since turned interactive.

checkpoint.prompt: An MLFQ has three queues: Q2 (highest), Q1 and Q0 (lowest). The allotment at each level is 10 ms and there is no priority boost. Job A arrives at t = 0, needs 200 ms of CPU and runs alone on the machine. Name the queue A occupies at each moment, written as `Q2`, `Q1` or `Q0`.
checkpoint.explain: Rule 3 puts A at the top on arrival, and rule 4 drops it one level each time it spends a full 10 ms allotment, so it reaches the bottom after 20 ms and stays there - there is nowhere further to fall. The tempting answer for t = 150 is that A has fallen off the bottom or been penalised again, but the lowest queue is absorbing: from then on A simply round-robins with whatever else has sunk to join it.

guided-practice.prompt: Put these events in the order they occur when a user process performs a system call under limited direct execution.
fragments: The kernel, now in kernel mode, validates the arguments and performs the privileged work
The process, running in user mode, places a system-call number in a register and executes a trap instruction
The process resumes at the instruction after the trap, in user mode, with the result in a register
The hardware saves the caller's registers to its kernel stack, raises the privilege level, and jumps to the handler the trap table names for that number
The kernel executes return-from-trap, restoring the saved registers and lowering the privilege level
guided-practice.explain: The order is forced by who is privileged at each moment: the process cannot do the work itself, so it must trap first, and the trap must raise privilege and transfer control together or there would be an instant in which user code held kernel powers. Note that the process never names the handler's address - it names a number, and the trap table chosen at boot turns that number into an address. The common mistake is to imagine the trap as a function call into the kernel, which would put the destination under the caller's control and make the mode bit pointless.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete the description of how the kernel is entered safely. Each blank is a single word.
guided-practice.template:
At boot, in kernel mode, the OS installs a ___ table telling the hardware where to jump on each kind of trap.
A user process supplies a system-call ___ rather than an address.
The instruction that installs the table is itself ___.
guided-practice.explain: Every part of this exists to keep the set of kernel entry points fixed and small. If a process could pass an address it would jump into the middle of the kernel with privilege already raised, and the mode bit would protect nothing; a number indexes a list the OS itself wrote. The installation must in turn be privileged, or a process could simply rewrite the table and point an entry at its own code.

guided-practice.prompt: Three jobs arrive together at t = 0: A needs 100 ms, B needs 10 ms, C needs 10 ms. A FIFO scheduler runs them in the order A, B, C. Give each value in milliseconds.
guided-practice.explain: With every arrival at zero, turnaround is just completion time, so the three are 100, 110 and 120 for an average of 110. The response times are 0, 100 and 110, averaging 70 - and the gap between those two averages is the whole story of the convoy. B and C each do ten milliseconds of work and each spend about a hundred milliseconds behind A for no reason but arrival order. The tempting error is to average 100, 10 and 10, which is average **run** time and measures the workload rather than the scheduler.

guided-practice.prompt: A colleague proposes running each process by simply jumping to its first instruction and letting it go, on the grounds that anything else is slower. Explain the two distinct problems this creates, name the mechanism that solves each, and say why the fast path survives both.
guided-practice.explain: Your colleague is right about speed, and that is exactly why the design keeps direct execution and merely limits it. The first problem is restricted operations: a process needs I/O but must not be allowed to touch devices directly, solved by the mode bit plus a trap instruction that raises privilege and jumps to a boot-installed table entry in one step. The second is regaining control, a different problem with a different answer - waiting for the process to call back in is cooperative and fails against a loop that makes no calls, leaving reboot as the only remedy, so the OS arms a timer interrupt that fires regardless. The fast path survives both because neither mechanism sits between the process and the CPU: ordinary instructions still run unsupervised at full speed, and the cost is paid only at the boundary crossings.

scheduling-drills.prompt: The same three jobs arrive together at t = 0: A needs 100 ms, B needs 10 ms, C needs 10 ms. Now a Shortest Job First scheduler runs them. Give each value in milliseconds.
scheduling-drills.explain: The average turnaround falls from 110 to 50 without the machine doing a single instruction less - only the order changed. A pays for it, rising from 100 to 120, and that is the bargain SJF strikes: it makes one long job slightly worse off to make several short jobs dramatically better off, which lowers the mean because the mean is dominated by how many jobs waited rather than by how long any one of them ran.

scheduling-drills.prompt: Job A arrives at t = 0 and needs 100 ms. Jobs B and C both arrive at t = 10 and each need 10 ms. Compare non-pre-emptive Shortest Job First, which never interrupts a running job, with Shortest Time-to-Completion First, which re-decides whenever a job arrives. Ties are broken in favour of B. Give each turnaround time in milliseconds.
scheduling-drills.explain: Under SJF, A is already running when B and C turn up, and a non-pre-emptive scheduler is committed: B finishes at 110 having arrived at 10, giving 100, and C finishes at 120 for 110, an average of 103.33 against STCF's 50. STCF stops A at t = 10, clears both short jobs by t = 30 and returns to A, so B and C get turnarounds of 10 and 20 while A rises to 120. The point is that SJF's optimality depends entirely on all jobs arriving together, and the moment they do not, pre-emption - which exists only because the timer interrupt exists - is what recovers it.

scheduling-drills.prompt: Three jobs arrive together at t = 0, each needing exactly 5 ms. Compare round robin with a 1 ms quantum, cycling A, B, C, against SJF running them in the order A, B, C. Ignore context-switch cost. Give each value in milliseconds.
scheduling-drills.explain: Round robin's first runs are at 0, 1 and 2, so response averages 1 against SJF's 5; but the jobs now complete at 13, 14 and 15 rather than 5, 10 and 15, so turnaround rises from 10 to 14. This is not a flaw in this particular example. Any policy that shares the CPU evenly in the short term pushes every job's completion towards the end of the run, so it is close to the worst possible policy for turnaround precisely because it is the best for response. The tempting reading is that round robin is simply better because everyone starts sooner - it is better at one metric, and the same mechanism is what makes it worse at the other.

scheduling-drills.prompt: Three jobs, each needing 12 ms of CPU, run under round robin with quantum q. A context switch costs 1 ms and one occurs between each pair of consecutive time slices, but not after the final slice. Give the number of context switches and the total elapsed time in milliseconds.
scheduling-drills.explain: With q = 2 each job takes six slices, so there are eighteen slices and seventeen switches, and 36 ms of real work costs 53 ms of machine time - nearly a third of the CPU spent switching rather than computing. At q = 4 that overhead falls to 8 ms, and at q = 12 the policy has degenerated into FIFO with just 2 ms. This is why the quantum is not simply made as small as possible: the switch cost is amortised over the slice, so halving the quantum roughly doubles the overhead. Real systems also pay a larger indirect cost - caches and TLB entries belonging to the wrong process - which this arithmetic does not even include.

scheduling-drills.prompt: Put these events in the order they occur when a timer interrupt causes the OS to switch from process A to process B.
fragments: The scheduler decides that B should run instead of A
The timer fires, and the hardware saves A's user registers onto A's kernel stack, raises the privilege level and jumps to the interrupt handler
Process B resumes in user mode at the instruction it was interrupted on earlier
Return-from-trap pops B's user registers from B's kernel stack and lowers the privilege level
The switch routine saves A's kernel registers into A's process structure and restores B's from B's, switching the stack pointer last
scheduling-drills.explain: The two saves happen at different times and by different agents, and the order tells you why. The hardware save comes first because it must happen before any OS instruction runs, otherwise the handler would destroy the very state it is meant to preserve. The software save comes after the scheduling decision, because there is no point saving kernel context if the answer turns out to be 'keep running A'. Switching the stack pointer is the pivot: from that instruction onwards the kernel is executing on B's stack, which is why the return-from-trap that follows finds B's registers rather than A's.

policy-design.prompt: An MLFQ has three queues: Q2 (highest), Q1 and Q0 (lowest). The allotment at each level is 10 ms, the lowest queue round-robins with a 10 ms quantum, and there is no priority boost. Job A arrives at t = 0 and needs 200 ms. Job B arrives at t = 100 and needs 20 ms. Neither performs I/O. Answer with a queue name, a job name or a number of milliseconds as appropriate.

steps.label: CPU time A has received by t = 120

policy-design.explain: A sinks to Q0 by t = 20 because it spends a full allotment at each of the two levels above, and then runs undisturbed until B arrives. Rule 3 admits B at the top, so rule 1 pre-empts A immediately - which is the entire point: the scheduler has no idea B is short, but assuming it is costs at most one allotment if the guess turns out wrong. B spends 10 ms in Q2, drops to Q1, spends its second 10 ms there and finishes at 120 with a turnaround of 20 rather than the 120 that FIFO would have given it. A has still received exactly the 100 ms it ran before B arrived; being pre-empted delays a job but never takes completed work back.

policy-design.prompt: The same MLFQ - three queues Q2, Q1, Q0, a 10 ms allotment at each level, a 10 ms round-robin quantum in Q0 - now applies rule 5, a priority boost every S = 50 ms that moves every job to Q2 and resets its allotment. Job A arrives at t = 0 needing 100 ms; job B arrives at t = 25 needing 100 ms. Where both sit in Q0, A is ahead of B in the round-robin order. Answer with a queue name, a job name or a number of milliseconds.

steps.label: CPU time A has received by t = 50
CPU time B has received by t = 50

policy-design.explain: A has already sunk to Q0 by t = 20, so B's arrival at the top pre-empts it at once, and B spends 25 to 35 in Q2 and 35 to 45 in Q1 before joining A at the bottom. A then runs from 45 until the boost, having accumulated 25 + 5 = 30 ms against B's 20. The boost at t = 50 is the interesting line: without it, a steady stream of new arrivals would keep the upper queues occupied and A could starve indefinitely, since rule 1 never looks at a lower queue while a higher one is non-empty. Resetting everyone to Q2 guarantees a lower bound on progress and, as a bonus, forgives a job whose behaviour has changed from CPU-bound to interactive.

policy-design.prompt: A hobby operating system schedules processes only when they make a system call, on the assumption that every program will call `yield` periodically. It runs beautifully for weeks. Then a user compiles a program containing `while (1) { x++; }`, runs it, and the machine stops responding entirely - the shell, the clock and the network all freeze, and only the reset button helps. Name the cause and explain why the design made this outcome inevitable.
policy-design.explain: The scheduler is cooperative, so the OS regains the CPU only when a process hands it back through a system call, and this loop makes none - no I/O, no `yield`, not even a memory allocation. The OS is therefore not running, and code that is not running cannot schedule anything, which is why every other subsystem freezes with it rather than just the offending program. The tempting diagnosis is a bug in the loop or a priority inversion, but nothing is wrong with the program at all: it is a perfectly legal computation, and a design that depends on every program being polite has no defence against an impolite one that need not even be malicious. The fix is structural rather than a patch to the scheduler - arm a hardware timer at boot so that an interrupt returns control on a fixed period whether the process cooperates or not.

policy-design.prompt: An MLFQ implements rule 4 as: a job that uses its entire time slice drops one queue, but a job that relinquishes the CPU before its slice ends keeps its current priority. A developer notices that their batch job runs far faster if, just before each 10 ms slice would expire, it issues a 1 ms read of a file it does not need. Long-running jobs on the same machine now make almost no progress. Name what the developer is doing and explain the flaw in rule 4 that permits it.
policy-design.explain: Rule 4 as written infers 'interactive' from a single observation - did this job finish its slice? - and that observation is entirely under the job's control. By giving up the CPU with a millisecond to spare, the job never once uses a whole slice, so it never sinks, and it retains top priority while consuming roughly ninety per cent of every slice it is given. Rule 1 then does the rest: while a top-queue job is runnable the genuinely long jobs below it are never even considered, so they starve. The tempting reading is that the developer found a clever optimisation, but the gain is taken directly from the other jobs and nothing on the machine goes faster in aggregate. The repair lies in the accounting rather than the rule: track the total CPU time a job has consumed at its current level and demote it once that reaches the allotment, however many times it relinquished the CPU along the way.

policy-design.prompt: You are specifying the CPU scheduler for a developer workstation that concurrently runs a compile farm of long batch jobs, an interactive shell, and a video call that must not stutter. Argue for a multi-level feedback queue. State which metric each of the three workloads actually cares about; explain why FIFO, SJF, STCF and plain round robin each fail on at least one of them, including the fact that SJF and STCF need a job's length in advance; give the rules your scheduler uses, including how allotment is accounted for and why, and how you would choose the boost period and the quantum; and be honest about what each choice costs. There are no tests here: your answer is marked against a rubric of the points it must cover.
policy-design.explain: The argument has a shape worth learning. The three workloads want different numbers: the compile farm wants low average turnaround, the shell and the call want low response time, and no single figure describes all three. FIFO delivers the convoy - a thirty-second compile in front of a keystroke - while SJF and STCF give excellent turnaround but require an oracle that says how long each job will run, which no real OS has, and both still make the video call wait behind whatever is running. Round robin fixes response and ruins turnaround by stretching every job to the end of the run. The MLFQ replaces the oracle with observation: admit every job at the top optimistically, demote it when it spends its allotment at a level, and let jobs that block for I/O stay high without any special case for them. Account allotment as total CPU time consumed at that level rather than as slices completed, or a job games the scheduler by relinquishing the CPU a millisecond early forever. Boost every job to the top periodically, with $S$ chosen short enough that a long job's worst-case wait is tolerable and long enough that it does not throw away the classification you spent effort learning. Choose a quantum that amortises the context switch - a few milliseconds, tens or hundreds of times the switch cost - and say plainly that a shorter one buys response and spends the machine on switching and cold caches. An answer that stops at 'use an MLFQ' has skipped every interesting half.

exam.prompt: What is a job's turnaround time?
choices: The time from the job's arrival until it first runs
The time from the job's arrival until it completes
The time the job spends actually executing on the CPU
The interval between two consecutive context switches
exam.explain: Turnaround is $T_{completion} - T_{arrival}$, so it includes every millisecond the job spent waiting for someone else. The first option is response time, and confusing the two is the mistake this whole floor is built around - a job can have superb response and dreadful turnaround, which is exactly what round robin produces. The third describes run time, a property of the job rather than of the scheduler, and no scheduling policy can improve it.

exam.prompt: Which of these happen during a context switch triggered by a timer interrupt? Select all that apply.
choices: The hardware saves the interrupted process's user registers onto its kernel stack
Software saves the outgoing process's kernel registers into its process structure
The kernel stack pointer is switched to the incoming process's kernel stack
The outgoing process's program is reloaded from disk
exam.explain: Register state is saved twice by two different agents, and the stack-pointer swap is the pivot between outgoing and incoming process. Nothing is read from disk: the outgoing process's memory stays exactly where it is, which is what makes a switch cost microseconds rather than milliseconds - and it is also why the real expense is indirect, in the caches and TLB entries the incoming process now finds full of the wrong data.

exam.prompt: Complete the two scheduling metrics. Each blank is a single word drawn from `arrival`, `completion`, `first_run`.
exam.explain: Both metrics subtract arrival, because both ask how long the job has been waiting from the user's point of view rather than from the machine's. What differs is the end point, and that single difference is what pulls scheduling policies in opposite directions: shortening the wait before the first run means switching often, and switching often pushes every completion later.

exam.prompt: Four jobs run under Shortest Time-to-Completion First on one CPU. A arrives at t = 0 needing 10 ms, B arrives at t = 2 needing 4 ms, C arrives at t = 4 needing 1 ms, D arrives at t = 6 needing 5 ms. Put the jobs in the order they complete.
fragments: A (arrives at 0, needs 10 ms)
B (arrives at 2, needs 4 ms)
C (arrives at 4, needs 1 ms)
D (arrives at 6, needs 5 ms)
exam.explain: STCF compares remaining time, not original length, and re-decides on every arrival. A runs from 0 to 2 and is pre-empted by B, which has 4 left against A's 8; C arrives at 4 with 1 against B's remaining 2, so C pre-empts and finishes at 5; B resumes and finishes at 7; D, arriving at 6 with 5, beats A's remaining 8 and finishes at 12; A finishes last, at 20. Sorting by original length happens to give the same answer here, which is the trap - it is remaining time that decides, and A's early two milliseconds are exactly the sort of thing that makes the two rules diverge.

exam.prompt: Three jobs arrive together at t = 0: A needs 8 ms, B needs 4 ms, C needs 4 ms. Compare round robin with a 2 ms quantum, cycling A, B, C, against FIFO running them in the order A, B, C. Ignore context-switch cost. Give each value in milliseconds.

steps.label: round robin: completion time of B
round robin: completion time of A

exam.explain: The round-robin schedule is A, B, C, A, B, C, A, A in 2 ms slices, so B completes at 10, C at 12 and A at 16, with first runs at 0, 2 and 4 for an average response of 2. FIFO completes at 8, 12 and 16 for an average turnaround of 12, against round robin's 12.67 - slightly worse, as always - while C's response falls from 12 to 4. Notice how small the turnaround penalty is compared with the earlier example of three equal 5 ms jobs: when the jobs are of comparable length there is less for round robin to spoil, which is the practical reason it is a reasonable default in a queue of similar tasks and a poor one in a queue containing a single giant job.

exam.prompt: An MLFQ has three queues Q2 (highest), Q1 and Q0 (lowest), an allotment of 10 ms at each level, a 10 ms round-robin quantum in Q0 and no priority boost. Jobs A and B both arrive at t = 0, each needing 200 ms, and A is ahead of B in every queue's round-robin order. Neither performs I/O. Answer with a queue name, a job name or a number of milliseconds.

steps.label: CPU time A has received by t = 60

exam.explain: Rule 2 alternates them at each level: A takes 0 to 10 in Q2 and drops, B takes 10 to 20 and drops, A takes 20 to 30 in Q1 and drops, B takes 30 to 40 and drops, and from 40 onwards both round-robin in Q0. The trap is answering Q0 for A at t = 25 - A has been demoted once, not twice, because B held the CPU between 10 and 20, and demotion is charged for CPU time consumed rather than for wall-clock time elapsed. By t = 60 A has run three slices of 10 ms, for a total of 30.

exam.prompt: Explain why lowering the time-slice length improves average response time but worsens both average turnaround time and the machine's throughput. Say what actually bounds how small a useful quantum can be.
exam.explain: A shorter quantum means every runnable job gets its first slice sooner, so response falls - it is bounded below by roughly the quantum times the number of runnable jobs. The same evenness is what harms turnaround: sharing the CPU finely stretches every job across the whole run so that completions cluster at the end instead of arriving one at a time, and a policy that is perfectly fair in the short term is close to the worst possible one for average turnaround. Throughput is a separate loss, because every slice boundary is a context switch that does no useful work; the switch cost is amortised over the slice, so as the quantum approaches that cost the fraction of the machine spent switching approaches a half. The real bound is tighter than the arithmetic suggests, because the direct cost of saving registers is dwarfed by the indirect cost of resuming a process whose cache and TLB entries have been evicted by whoever ran in between.

exam.prompt: A media appliance runs about twenty threads. Its scheduler currently uses a 200 ms round-robin quantum, chosen because a context switch costs roughly 0.2 ms and the team wanted overhead under one part in a thousand. Users report that button presses take up to four seconds to register, though throughput measurements look excellent. Assess the team's reasoning, recommend a quantum, and say what your recommendation costs and what it does not fix.
exam.explain: The team optimised the one metric their measurements showed. With twenty threads and a 200 ms quantum, worst-case response is nineteen slices of waiting - about 3.8 seconds - which matches the complaint exactly, so the fault is not a bug anywhere but the quantum itself. A few milliseconds is the right order: at 5 ms the worst case falls below 100 ms while overhead rises to about 0.2 in 5.2, roughly four per cent, which is a real cost and should be stated rather than hidden, and the indirect cache and TLB cost makes the true figure higher still. The deeper point is that no single quantum serves both a decoder thread that wants throughput and a button handler that wants response, so the honest recommendation is a shorter quantum **and** priorities - an MLFQ that lets the interactive threads stay near the top while the batch work sinks - with a boost so that the sunk threads cannot starve. Changing the quantum alone improves the worst case but still gives every thread an equal share whether it needs one or not.

sections.title: Every process wakes up at address zero
sections.body:
A program compiled on your machine believes its first instruction lives at some fixed address and that its heap grows upward from a place it was told about at link time. Run two copies of it at once and both believe exactly the same thing, yet they must not touch the same physical bytes. The **address space** is the operating system's answer: each process is handed a private, contiguous-looking range of addresses starting at zero, and the OS keeps the map from that fiction to real memory.

The reason is not politeness. Early machines ran one program at a time in real memory, and the moment more than one process shares a machine you need three things at once - **relocation**, so a program can be placed anywhere; **protection**, so one process cannot read or scribble on another; and **transparency**, so the program need not know any of this happened.

**Base and bounds** delivers all three with two registers. The base register holds where this process's memory actually starts; the bounds register holds how large its address space is. On every reference the hardware checks `virt < bounds` and then computes `base + virt`. That is it - an add and a compare, cheap enough to sit in the critical path of every load and store.

The virtual address is therefore never a real address, and the illusion is maintained by hardware the process cannot see. Change the base register and the whole process moves, physically, without a single instruction in it noticing - which is precisely what makes moving a running process possible at all. The cost is that the entire address space must live in one contiguous physical run, and we are about to find out why that is expensive.

annotations.text: The check comes first - translating and then checking would leak one access outside the address space. Note the `>=`: with bounds 4096 the legal virtual addresses are 0 to 4095.
One addition. Every load, store and instruction fetch pays exactly this.

checkpoint.prompt: A process runs with base = 32768 and bounds = 4096. Give the physical address for each virtual address, or write `fault` if the reference is illegal.
checkpoint.explain: Every legal translation is the same single addition, so the arithmetic is never the hard part - the boundary is. Bounds is a size, not a largest legal address, so 4095 is the last byte inside the space and 4096 is one past the end. Reading bounds as an address is the standard off-by-one here, and it is the same mistake that turns a safe loop into a buffer overrun.

sections.title: One base is one too few
sections.body:
Base and bounds relocates the address space as one lump, and that lump is mostly nothing. Code sits at the bottom, the heap grows upward above it, the stack grows downward from the top, and between them lies a vast unused hole that exists so that both may grow. A process with a 16 KB address space using 2 KB of code, 3 KB of heap and 2 KB of stack still costs 16 KB of physical memory, because the hole is copied too.

**Segmentation** is the obvious repair: give each logically distinct region its own base and bounds pair instead of one for the whole space. Now the hole is never placed anywhere, because it is not part of any segment. A virtual address is split - here the top two bits name the segment and the rest is an offset within it - and the hardware indexes a small segment table to find that segment's base and size.

The stack needs one extra bit of state, because it grows the wrong way. Its offsets count backwards from the top of the segment, so the hardware subtracts the segment size from the offset to get a negative displacement and adds that to the base. Address 15360 in a 16 KB space is 1024 bytes below the top, so with a stack base of 28672 it lands at 27648.

Segmentation also makes sharing natural - two processes can point their code segment at the same physical bytes, marked read-only - and it makes out-of-bounds faults precise, since running off the end of the heap is caught by the heap's own size. What it does not fix is the shape of what it asks for. Physical memory now holds segments of every conceivable size, and when they come and go they leave gaps: this is **external fragmentation**, and it is the reason the next two sections exist.

annotations.text: Two bits give four segment numbers; this table leaves entry 2 unused, so addresses in it fault.
`virt >> 12` on a 14-bit address yields 0, 1, 2 or 3 - the segment number.
The negative-offset trick: 15360 & 0xFFF is 3072, and 3072 - 4096 = -1024.

checkpoint.prompt: Using the segment table above (code base 32768 size 2048; heap base 34816 size 3072; stack base 28672 size 2048, growing down), translate these 14-bit virtual addresses. Write `fault` if the reference is illegal.
checkpoint.explain: Strip the top two bits to get the offset, check it against that segment's own size, then add that segment's own base: 4200 is heap offset 104, so 34816 + 104 = 34920. 7500 is heap offset 3404, which is past the heap's 3072 bytes even though the address is comfortably inside the 16 KB address space - the whole point of segmentation is that each region is bounded separately, so a legal-looking address can still be illegal.

sections.title: Managing the holes
sections.body:
Once memory is handed out in variable-sized pieces, the allocator's real job is bookkeeping the gaps. A **free list** records each unused run as an address and a length. Satisfying a request means finding a run large enough and **splitting** it: the request takes the front, and what remains stays on the list as a smaller free block. Freeing does the reverse - **coalescing** - because two adjacent free runs that stay separate can never together serve a request larger than either.

Which run to split is a policy, and the three classical answers all lose somewhere. **First fit** takes the first block that is large enough: fast, no scan of the whole list, but it chews up the blocks near the head of the list. **Best fit** takes the smallest block that is large enough: it wastes the least on this request, but must scan everything and leaves behind slivers too small ever to be used. **Worst fit** takes the largest block, on the theory that the leftover will be big enough to be useful - in practice it also scans everything, and destroys the large blocks you were saving.

The `malloc` header is what makes freeing possible at all. `free(ptr)` is given one pointer and no size, so the allocator stores the block's size in a small header immediately before the returned pointer and steps backwards to read it. That is also why asking for one byte costs rather more than one byte.

No policy escapes the underlying problem. With variable sizes, memory that is free but scattered cannot satisfy a large request: an allocator can hold 40 KB free in six pieces and still fail a 12 KB request. Coalescing helps only where the free runs happen to touch. External fragmentation is not a bug in a policy - it is what variable-sized allocation is.

annotations.text: The header the allocator hides just below every returned pointer; `free` reads the size back from it.
Split only if the remainder can hold a header and at least one usable byte - otherwise hand over the whole block.
The split itself: this block shrinks to the requested size, and the rest becomes a new free block.

checkpoint.prompt: A free list holds three blocks in address order: 20 bytes at address 1000, 15 bytes at 2000, 30 bytes at 3000. A request for 12 bytes arrives (ignore header overhead). Give the **address** of the block each policy chooses.
checkpoint.explain: First fit stops at the first block that fits and leaves an 8-byte remainder; best fit scans the whole list for the tightest fit, the 15-byte block, and leaves a 3-byte sliver that will probably never be used again; worst fit takes the 30-byte block and leaves 18. The tempting reading is that best fit is simply best - it does waste least on this request, but it is the policy that manufactures the slivers, and it pays a full scan of the list to do it.

sections.title: Fixed-size pieces, and the table they need
sections.body:
External fragmentation comes from variable sizes, so **paging** removes variable sizes. Physical memory is cut into fixed-size **page frames**, the address space into **pages** of the same size, and any page may go in any frame. A request for a page can now be satisfied by any free frame at all, so a free frame list never needs a fit policy and placement never fails while frames remain.

Translation is no longer arithmetic but a lookup. A virtual address splits into a **virtual page number** and an **offset**: with 4 KB pages the low 12 bits are the offset and everything above is the VPN. The VPN indexes the process's **page table** to find the **physical frame number**; the offset is copied through untouched, because a page and a frame are the same size and a byte's position within them is identical. So 0x00003ABC has VPN 0x3 and offset 0xABC, and if the page table maps page 3 to frame 0x1F the physical address is 0x1FABC - the offset digits are literally the same digits.
