Two costs replace the one that was removed. The first is **internal fragmentation**: a process needing 4097 bytes gets two whole pages, and the last 4095 bytes of the second are wasted inside the allocation rather than between allocations. It is bounded by under one page per region, which is a far better bargain than an unbounded external hole.

The second is size, and it is severe. A 32-bit address space with 4 KB pages has $2^{20}$ pages, so a page table with a 4-byte entry each is 4 MB - **per process**. A hundred processes would need 400 MB of page tables before running a single instruction, and unlike two segment registers this cannot live in the CPU, so it sits in memory and every translation now costs an extra memory reference. Later floors spend themselves entirely on undoing those two costs.

annotations.text: A shift, not a division: the VPN is simply the address with the offset bits discarded.
The mask keeps the low 12 bits - the byte's position within its page.
This is the extra memory reference paging costs on every access, and the reason the TLB exists.
The offset is OR'd in unchanged. Only the page-number half of the address is ever translated.

checkpoint.prompt: Complete the two lines that split a 32-bit virtual address into its page number and its offset, for 4096-byte pages.
checkpoint.template:
uint32_t vpn    = virt ___ 12;
uint32_t offset = virt ___ 0xFFF;
checkpoint.explain: The offset is the low 12 bits because $2^{12} = 4096$, so masking with 0xFFF keeps exactly the position within the page, and shifting right by 12 discards those bits to leave the page number. Swapping the two is the common slip: masking the address with 0xFFF tells you where in the page, never which page.

guided-practice.prompt: A process is loaded with base = 32768 and bounds = 4096. For each virtual address give the physical address the hardware produces, or `fault` if the reference is rejected.
guided-practice.explain: Each legal address is base + virtual and nothing more, which is why base-and-bounds costs one add per reference. 5000 is refused not because there is no memory there - the machine has plenty - but because this process was promised only 4096 bytes, and the bounds register is that promise. The physical addresses from 36864 upwards are perfectly real and may well belong to another process; the check is what stops this one reaching them.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete the bounds check and the translation in the MMU's relocation path. The first blank is a comparison operator, the second an arithmetic operator.
guided-practice.explain: Bounds is the **size** of the address space, so the legal virtual addresses are 0 through bounds - 1 and the fault condition is `>=`. Writing `>` admits one byte past the end, which is exactly the kind of one-byte overrun that lets a process read the beginning of its neighbour. The translation is an addition rather than a subtraction because a virtual address is a displacement from the start of the process's memory, and base is where that start physically is.

guided-practice.prompt: A 14-bit address space (16 KB) uses segmentation. The top two bits select the segment: 00 code (base 32768, size 2048), 01 heap (base 34816, size 3072), 11 stack (base 28672, size 2048, growing downwards). Translate each virtual address, writing `fault` for an illegal reference.
guided-practice.explain: Heap addresses give up their top two bits and are checked against 3072: 4200 is offset 104 and 7000 is offset 2904, both legal, while 7500 is offset 3404 and runs off the end of the heap. The stack is the one that catches people. Its offsets are negative displacements from the base: 15360 has offset 3072, which becomes 3072 - 4096 = -1024, so the physical address is 28672 - 1024 = 27648. By the same rule 14000 has offset 1712, hence -2384, which is further below the base than the stack's 2048 bytes allow - a legal-looking address in the middle of the space, rejected because each segment is bounded on its own.

guided-practice.prompt: A colleague argues that segmentation is pointless because base-and-bounds already relocates a process anywhere in physical memory. Explain what segmentation buys, using the shape of a real address space to make the case, and name the cost it introduces.
guided-practice.explain: An address space is sparse by design: the hole between the heap and the stack exists so that both can grow, and under base-and-bounds that hole is copied into physical memory byte for byte, so a process using 7 KB of a 16 KB space still occupies 16 KB. Segmentation places each region separately, so nothing is reserved for the hole, and it gains precise per-region bounds and the ability to share a read-only code segment between processes. The tempting objection - that both schemes relocate equally well - is true and beside the point; relocation was never the thing being paid for. The cost is that physical memory now holds runs of many different sizes, and as segments come and go the free space breaks into scattered gaps that no single large request can use.

translation-drills.prompt: A 64-byte address space is divided into 16-byte pages, so a virtual address is 6 bits: 2 bits of VPN and 4 bits of offset. The page table is `[3, 7, 5, 2]`, mapping page 0 to frame 3, page 1 to frame 7, page 2 to frame 5 and page 3 to frame 2. Give the physical address for each virtual address, in decimal.
translation-drills.explain: Split, look up, recombine. Virtual 21 is 010101: VPN 01 is page 1, offset 0101 is 5, page 1 lives in frame 7, so the physical address is 7 x 16 + 5 = 117. Virtual 63 is the highest address in the space and lands at 2 x 16 + 15 = 47, which is **lower** than where virtual 0 lands - a good demonstration that paging preserves no ordering at all between virtual and physical addresses. Multiplying the whole virtual address by something, or adding a base to it, is the habit left over from the previous two schemes and gives the wrong answer every time.

translation-drills.prompt: A 32-bit virtual address space uses 4 KB pages, so the low 12 bits are the offset. Virtual address 0x00003ABC is translated, and the page table entry for its page holds frame number 0x1F with the valid bit set. Answer in hexadecimal with a `0x` prefix, except for the final step which is a decimal count.

steps.label: how many bits of the virtual address the translation replaced

translation-drills.explain: With 4 KB pages the offset is exactly the low three hex digits, since each hex digit is 4 bits and 12 / 4 = 3 - which is why paging is so much easier to read in hexadecimal than in decimal. The offset digits ABC are carried through untouched and only the page-number half is replaced, giving 0x1FABC. The last step is the point of the exercise: 20 of the 32 bits are translated and 12 are not, so the page table's entire job is mapping one 20-bit number to another.

translation-drills.prompt: Put the steps the hardware takes on a single memory reference under paging into the order in which they actually happen.
fragments: Read the page table entry at that location, which is a real memory access
Extract the VPN from the top bits of the virtual address
Concatenate the frame number with the untranslated offset
Check the entry's valid bit and raise a fault if it is clear
Add the VPN, scaled by the entry size, to the page table base register
Issue the access to the resulting physical address
translation-drills.explain: The VPN has to be extracted before it can be used as an index, the index has to be turned into an address using the page table base register before anything can be read, and the valid bit must be checked before the frame number is trusted - checking after the access would be checking too late. The step that surprises people is the third: the page table lives in memory, so every translated reference costs a second, hidden memory access, and that cost is what motivates every mechanism on the floors that follow.

translation-drills.prompt: Fill in the arithmetic for the size of a linear page table on a 32-bit address space with 4 KB pages and 4-byte page table entries. Give the first two blanks as plain integers (the exponents), and the last as a whole number of megabytes.
translation-drills.template:
pages    = 2^32 / 2^12 = 2^___
PT bytes = 2^___ * 4 = ___ MB per process
translation-drills.explain: Dividing the address space by the page size counts the pages: $2^{32}/2^{12} = 2^{20}$, just over a million. Every one of those pages needs an entry whether or not the process ever touches it, because the table is indexed directly by page number, so the table costs $2^{20} \times 4 = 4$ MB for every process on the machine. A hundred processes would burn 400 MB of page tables before executing an instruction - and the fact that almost every one of those entries is invalid is exactly what the later multi-level schemes exploit.

memory-design.prompt: A 100-byte heap starts as one free block: address 0, length 100. Ignore header overhead, and assume the allocator uses first fit and splits from the front of the block it chooses. After each operation, give the free list as `addr:len` pairs separated by a comma and a space, in address order.
memory-design.explain: Each allocation splits the front off the free block and the remainder stays on the list, so the single block simply walks forward and shrinks. The last two steps are where coalescing earns its keep: freeing the block at 20 puts a 30-byte run back on a list with no free neighbour, but freeing the block at 0 produces a run that ends exactly where that one begins, so the two merge into 0:50. Left unmerged they would be a 20 and a 30 that could never together serve a 40-byte request, even with 50 contiguous bytes sitting free.

memory-design.prompt: A long-running server allocates and frees objects of many different sizes. After several days, `malloc(12288)` fails. Instrumenting the allocator shows 40 KB of free space spread over six blocks, the largest of which is 10 KB, and the process is nowhere near its memory limit. Name the cause and explain why simply having more free space would not necessarily fix it.
memory-design.explain: An allocator can only satisfy a request from a single contiguous run, so 40 KB free in six pieces of at most 10 KB cannot serve a 12 KB request - the space exists but not in the shape required. Coalescing only merges free blocks that are physically adjacent, and here the free blocks are separated by live allocations, so nothing merges. The tempting diagnosis is a leak, because the symptom is a failing allocation in a long-running process, but a leak would show the free total shrinking, whereas here the free total stays healthy while the largest block does not. This is the unavoidable consequence of variable-sized allocation, and adding memory only postpones it.

memory-design.prompt: You are specifying the memory subsystem for a small operating system on a 32-bit machine that must run dozens of processes of unpredictable size. Argue for fixed-size paging over segmentation. State which problem the fixed size removes and why, name the new form of waste it introduces and what bounds it, describe how a virtual address is split and translated, and be honest about the space cost of a linear page table with worked numbers for 4 KB pages and 4-byte entries. There are no tests here: your answer is marked against a rubric of the points it must cover.
memory-design.hint: Work outwards from one sentence: external fragmentation is caused by variable sizes, so make every piece the same size. Then account honestly for what that decision costs.
memory-design.explain: The argument has a shape worth learning. External fragmentation exists because a request must be met by one contiguous run of exactly the size asked for; make every piece the same size and any free frame serves any request, so placement never fails while frames remain and no fit policy is needed at all. The new waste is internal - the tail of the last page of each region - but it is bounded by under one page per region rather than being unbounded and scattered, which is a far better bargain. Translation becomes a lookup rather than an addition: the top 20 bits index the page table for a frame number and the low 12 bits pass through untouched. The honest part is the cost: $2^{20}$ entries at 4 bytes is 4 MB of page table per process, so dozens of processes cost hundreds of megabytes, and the table lives in memory so each reference costs a second one. An answer that stops at 'paging is better' has skipped the only interesting half.

exam.prompt: What is a process's address space?
choices: The private range of addresses, starting at zero, that a process sees, mapped by the OS onto real memory
The set of physical memory addresses the process currently occupies
The region of the kernel that stores a process's registers between context switches
The largest amount of memory the process is permitted to allocate
exam.explain: The defining property is that it is a fiction: it always begins at zero, it is the same fiction for every process, and the mapping onto physical memory is maintained by hardware the process cannot observe. The second option describes the physical footprint, which is exactly the thing the address space hides - and the two need not even be contiguous once paging is in play.

exam.prompt: Which of these are true of paging with fixed-size pages? Select all that apply.
choices: Any free physical frame can hold any page
It eliminates external fragmentation of physical memory
It can waste space inside the last page of a region
It makes a linear page table smaller than a segment table
exam.explain: Uniform size is what makes any frame interchangeable, and interchangeability is what removes external fragmentation - there is no longer such a thing as a gap of the wrong size. The waste moves inside the allocation instead, into the tail of the final page. The last option inverts the truth: a segment table has a handful of entries, while a linear page table has one per page of the address space whether used or not, which is precisely the problem paging creates.

exam.prompt: A process has base = 65536 and bounds = 8192. Give the physical address for each virtual address, or `fault`.
exam.explain: Add the base, and reject anything not strictly below the bounds: 65536 + 8191 = 73727 is the last legal byte, and 8192 is one past the end of the space. If you produced 73728 for the third step you read bounds as the highest legal address rather than as a size, which is the same off-by-one that makes array loops overrun.

exam.prompt: Segmentation with the top two bits selecting the segment in a 14-bit space: 00 code (base 32768, size 2048), 01 heap (base 34816, size 3072), 11 stack (base 28672, size 2048, growing downwards). Translate each, writing `fault` for an illegal reference.
exam.explain: Virtual 1000 is code offset 1000, inside 2048, so 32768 + 1000 = 33768. Virtual 2048 is still segment 00 - the top two bits do not change until 4096 - and its offset 2048 is one past the code segment's size, so it faults even though nothing looks unusual about the address. Virtual 16383 is stack offset 4095, that is -1 from the base, so 28672 - 1 = 28671: the very top of the address space sits one byte below the stack's base in physical memory, which is what growing downwards means.

exam.prompt: A 32-bit address space with 4 KB pages. Virtual address 0x0000C123 is translated and the page table maps its page to frame 0x2A0, valid. Give hexadecimal answers with a `0x` prefix.
exam.explain: Three hex digits of offset, everything above is the page number, and the frame number simply takes the place of the page number: 0x2A0 followed by 123. It is worth noticing that the physical address here has more significant digits than the virtual one - the frame number is wider than the page number it replaced, which is exactly how a machine addresses more physical memory than any single process can see.

exam.prompt: Complete the two sentences about free space management with a single word each.
exam.template:
Carving a request out of a larger free block and leaving the remainder on the list is called ___.
Merging two free blocks that are physically adjacent into one larger block is called ___.
exam.explain: The pair is deliberately symmetric: allocation splits, freeing coalesces, and an allocator that does the first without the second grinds its free list into dust that can never serve a large request. Coalescing is only possible between blocks that touch, which is why it mitigates external fragmentation without ever curing it.

exam.prompt: Order these events so that they describe how external fragmentation arises in a segmented physical memory.
fragments: A new request for a large segment fails despite ample free space in total
Physical memory is filled with segments of many different sizes
Some segments are freed, leaving gaps scattered between the survivors
Later segments are placed in the gaps large enough to hold them, splitting them further
exam.explain: The sequence matters because each step makes the next worse: variable sizes produce gaps, gaps get partially reused, and the leftovers get smaller with every reuse until no single run is large enough for a big request. The failure at the end is not a shortage of memory, it is a shortage of contiguous memory - which is why the eventual answer is to stop requiring contiguity at all.

exam.prompt: Explain why paging eliminates external fragmentation while no segmentation policy can, and state precisely what paging costs in exchange. Refer to sizes, to what happens to the offset during translation, and to the size of a linear page table.
exam.explain: External fragmentation is a consequence of variable sizes rather than of any allocation policy, so no fit policy can remove it - best fit merely chooses which slivers to create. Fixed-size frames make every free frame interchangeable, so a request for n pages is satisfiable whenever n frames are free anywhere, contiguous or not. The exchange is threefold: internal waste in the tail of the last page, bounded at under one page per region; a translation that is now a table lookup rather than an addition, with the offset passing through untouched and only the page number replaced; and a linear page table of one entry per page of the address space, which for a 32-bit space with 4 KB pages and 4-byte entries is 4 MB per process, held in memory and therefore costing an extra memory reference on every access.

exam.prompt: An embedded team reports that their allocator behaves perfectly in testing but that devices in the field fail an allocation after roughly a fortnight of uptime, always for one large buffer, while total free memory stays around a third of the heap. They propose switching the allocator's policy from first fit to best fit. Assess the proposal and say what you would do instead.
exam.explain: The symptom is the signature of external fragmentation: the failure needs time to develop, it strikes the largest request, and the total free figure stays healthy while the largest contiguous run does not. Switching to best fit does not address that and may worsen it, because best fit leaves behind the smallest possible remainders - slivers too small to serve anything later - so the free space becomes even more finely divided. The productive answers all attack the variable sizes rather than the policy: allocate that large buffer once at start-up and keep it, serve the common sizes from fixed-size pools so those allocations become interchangeable, or track the largest free block as a health metric so the failure is predicted rather than discovered. Measuring the largest contiguous run instead of the free total is what turns this from a field failure into a monitored one.

sections.title: A cache for translations
sections.body:
Paging bought placement freedom at a brutal price: the page table lives in memory, so every load, store and instruction fetch now costs **two** memory references instead of one. A program does not run half as fast because it is doing twice the work - it runs half as fast because the second reference sits on the critical path of the first, and nothing can start until translation finishes.

The **translation lookaside buffer** is the repair, and its name is a historical accident: it is not a buffer at all but a small, fully associative hardware cache of recently used virtual-page-to-frame mappings, sitting inside the memory-management unit. Perhaps 64 to 1536 entries, each holding a VPN, a PFN, protection bits, a valid bit and - as we shall see - an address-space tag.

The two paths are worth learning as paths, not as facts. On a **hit** the hardware extracts the VPN, finds it in the TLB, checks the protection bits, glues the untranslated offset back on and issues exactly one memory reference: the page table is never touched. On a **miss** the hardware walks the page table, installs the resulting mapping in the TLB, and then **retries the same instruction** - which now hits. That retry is why a miss costs the walk and nothing more, and why the miss path can afford to be slow.

Who performs that walk is an architectural choice. CISC machines such as x86 do it in hardware: the CPU knows the page-table format and the register that points at it. RISC machines such as MIPS raise a TLB-miss trap and let the operating system do it in software, which is more flexible - the OS may use any data structure it likes - but demands care, since the miss handler's own code must never itself take a TLB miss.

annotations.text: Fully associative: every entry is compared against the VPN simultaneously, because there is no time to search.
The hit path in full. One memory reference, and the page table is not consulted at all.
The miss path's cost, in one line: the reference paging added and the TLB exists to avoid.
The retry. The instruction is re-executed from the top and this time takes the hit path - which is why a miss costs the walk, not the walk plus a special case.

checkpoint.prompt: State how many memory references a single data access costs in each situation. Count the reference that fetches the data itself.
checkpoint.explain: A hit costs exactly what an unpaged machine costs, because the mapping is already in silicon and the offset never needed translating. Every level of page table adds one reference to the miss path, and the data fetch is always one more on top - so a four-level walk is four table reads plus the datum, which is five. The tempting answer for the hit case is 2, from remembering that paging costs an extra reference; the whole point of the TLB is that on a hit it does not.

sections.title: Why it works at all: locality
sections.body:
A cache of 64 entries covering an address space of a million pages should be useless, and it would be, were programs not extraordinarily repetitive about which pages they touch. **Spatial locality** says that having touched one byte a program will shortly touch a nearby one, and since a page is large - 4096 bytes holds a thousand ints - a single TLB entry serves an enormous run of consecutive accesses. **Temporal locality** says that a page touched now is likely to be touched again soon, which is what keeps a loop body, its stack frame and its counters resident across thousands of iterations.

Watch a simple traversal. Twelve four-byte ints beginning at virtual address 76, on a machine with 16-byte pages: `a[0]` is alone at the tail of page 4, `a[1]` through `a[4]` fill page 5, `a[5]` through `a[8]` fill page 6, and `a[9]` through `a[11]` begin page 7. Four accesses miss, eight hit, and the program did nothing to earn it.

Three things the programmer did not choose change that number. **Page size**: at 32 bytes the same array spans two pages, not four, so the misses fall from four to two. **Alignment**: start the array at 76 rather than 64 and it straddles four pages instead of three, buying an extra miss for nothing. **Repetition**: run the loop a second time and, if the pages are still resident, it costs no misses at all - the first pass warmed the TLB for every pass after it.

The consequence is the number that matters in practice. **TLB reach** is entries multiplied by page size: the total quantity of memory the TLB can address without a miss. Sixty-four entries at 4 KB reach 256 KB, which a modern working set exceeds without trying. Raise the page size and reach rises with it - the same 64 entries with 2 MB pages reach 128 MB - which is why large-page support exists and why databases and virtual machines reach for it.

annotations.text: The array's virtual start address decides which pages it lands on, and nothing in the source says so.
One memory reference per iteration, and the TLB decides whether it costs one or two.
Four misses out of twelve. Every hit here was bought by spatial locality: the page fetched for one element served three more.

checkpoint.prompt: Fill in the TLB reach for each configuration. Reach is the number of entries multiplied by the page size.
checkpoint.template:
64 entries,   4 KB pages  ->  reach ___ KB
64 entries,   2 MB pages  ->  reach ___ MB
128 entries,  4 KB pages  ->  reach ___ KB
checkpoint.explain: Reach is a straight product, and the striking thing is which factor moves it: doubling the entries doubles the reach from 256 KB to 512 KB, while changing the page size from 4 KB to 2 MB multiplies it by 512. TLB entries are expensive silicon on the critical path so they grow slowly; page size is free to change and is therefore the lever actually used when a workload's working set outruns the TLB.

sections.title: Page tables that skip the holes
sections.body:
The TLB fixes the time cost of paging, not the space cost. A 32-bit address space with 4 KB pages and 4-byte entries needs a linear page table of $2^{20} \times 4$ bytes, which is 4 MB **per process**, and almost all of it describes pages that do not exist. Between the top of the heap and the bottom of the stack lies a vast invalid hole whose entries are dutifully stored, one per absent page.

A **multi-level page table** exploits exactly that sparsity. Chop the linear table into page-sized pieces and add one level above it - a **page directory** - with one entry per piece, saying whether that piece exists and, if so, which frame holds it. A piece describing only invalid pages is simply never allocated, and the directory entry is marked invalid instead. The table is now allocated in proportion to how much of the address space is used, not how large it is.

The arithmetic is worth doing once. On a 32-bit machine with 4 KB pages the address splits into 10 bits of directory index, 10 bits of table index and 12 bits of offset; the directory holds 1024 entries in one 4 KB page, and each page table maps 1024 pages, or 4 MB. A process using 4 MB at the bottom of its address space and 8 KB of stack at the very top needs the directory plus two page tables: **three pages, 12 KB**, in place of 4 MB. The cost is one more memory reference on every TLB miss - which is affordable precisely because the TLB makes misses rare.

An **inverted page table** attacks the same problem from the other end: instead of one table per process indexed by page, keep **one table for the whole machine** indexed by frame, each entry recording which process and which virtual page currently occupies it. Its size depends on physical memory alone - 4 GB of frames is a million entries, whatever the process count - but the index is now the wrong way round, so finding a translation means searching, and a hash table over the entries is bolted on to make that tolerable. Whichever structure you choose, the TLB is unchanged: it caches finished translations and does not care where they came from.

annotations.text: The top ten bits select one of 1024 directory entries; each covers 4 MB of the address space.
This is where the saving lives. An invalid directory entry means 4 MB of absent address space costs one entry, not 1024.
The second table read. Every level added trades space for one more reference on the miss path.
0x00402ABC divided by 0x400000 is 1, so the directory index is 1; the next ten bits are 2; the low twelve are copied through untouched.

checkpoint.prompt: A 32-bit virtual address is split into 10 bits of page-directory index, 10 bits of page-table index and 12 bits of offset. Give the **page-directory index** in decimal for each address.
checkpoint.explain: The directory index is the address shifted right by 22 bits, which is the same as asking which 4 MB region the address falls in: 0x402ABC is just past 4 MB, so it is region 1, and 0xC0001004 is 3 GB up, which is 3072 MB divided by 4 MB, or 768. Reading only the top **eight** bits because they look like a neat pair of hexadecimal digits is the usual slip - the split is 10/10/12 and cuts a hex digit in half, which is exactly why hexadecimal is awkward here.

sections.title: The TLB is not part of the address space
sections.body:
A TLB entry says "virtual page 5 lives in frame 130", and that sentence is only true of one process. Switch to another and its page 5 is somewhere else entirely, so the entries left behind are not stale in the sense of being out of date - they are actively **wrong**, and using them would hand one process another's memory. The hardware cannot notice, because a VPN alone carries no evidence of whose it is.

The blunt fix is to **flush** the whole TLB on every context switch, by clearing every valid bit. It is correct, it costs almost nothing to perform, and it is very expensive to live with: each process resumes with a cold TLB and pays a miss on every page it touches until its working set is re-established, and on a machine switching frequently the TLB may never get warm at all.

The better fix is to make the entries carry whose they are. An **address-space identifier** - the ASID, essentially a small process id - is stored in each TLB entry and compared against a current-ASID register on every lookup. Entries belonging to different processes now coexist, and a switch costs one register write rather than the loss of the entire cache. Because the field is small, typically 8 bits, the OS must recycle identifiers, and recycling one does require invalidating the entries that carry it.

ASIDs also make deliberate sharing expressible: two processes mapping the same read-only library page can hold two TLB entries with different ASIDs and the same PFN, and both are correct. Neither scheme touches the other hazard, though - within a single address space, if the OS unmaps a page, changes its permissions or reuses its frame, the TLB entry describing it is now a lie that the hardware will happily keep believing. Invalidating that entry is the operating system's job, which is why every architecture exposes an instruction to do it, and why a missed invalidation is one of the nastiest bugs in a kernel.

annotations.text: One instruction, and the entire cache of translations is gone. Correct, and the reason a frequently switching machine feels slow.
The whole switch cost with ASIDs: change which tag lookups match. Nothing is discarded.
The hazard neither scheme addresses: a page table edited underneath a live TLB entry. The kernel must invalidate that VPN by hand.

checkpoint.prompt: For each event on a machine with an ASID-tagged TLB, state whether the whole TLB must be flushed. Answer `yes` or `no`.

steps.label: an ordinary context switch between two running processes
the OS unmaps one page from the current process
an ASID is recycled and handed to a newly created process

checkpoint.explain: ASIDs exist precisely so that an ordinary switch is a register write rather than a flush, and unmapping one page needs one targeted invalidation of that VPN, not a wholesale flush - a sledgehammer would work there but would throw away every other valid translation. Recycling is the case people miss: the identifier is only 8 bits, so when it is reused the old process's entries carrying that tag will match the new process's lookups, and they must be cleared first.

guided-practice.prompt: A machine has 4 KB pages and a hardware-managed TLB. Walk the two paths: for each event, state what the hardware does next, choosing from `check protection`, `walk page table`, `retry instruction`, `raise fault`.

steps.label: the VPN is found in the TLB and the entry is valid
the VPN is not found in the TLB
the walk found a valid PTE and the mapping has been installed
the walk found a PTE with its valid bit clear

guided-practice.explain: The hit path still checks protection - a cached translation is not a licence to write a read-only page, and skipping that check would be a security hole rather than an optimisation. The miss path deliberately ends by re-executing the instruction rather than continuing from where it stopped, so there is only one translation path in the hardware and the second attempt simply hits. A PTE with the valid bit clear is an access to a page the process does not have, and that is a fault whatever the TLB says.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete the three lines that split a 32-bit virtual address for a two-level page table with 4 KB pages and 1024-entry tables. Give the two shift amounts in decimal and the offset mask in hexadecimal as `0x` followed by three digits.
guided-practice.explain: The offset is the low 12 bits because a 4 KB page holds 4096 bytes, and the table index starts immediately above it at bit 12. The directory index sits above the ten table-index bits, so it starts at bit 22 - not 20, which is the tempting answer from remembering that a 32-bit space has 2^20 pages and forgetting that those twenty bits are being split in half.

guided-practice.prompt: An array of 12 four-byte ints begins at virtual address 76. A loop reads every element once, in order, on a machine with 16-byte pages and a TLB that starts empty and has room for far more entries than this array needs. Give each count as a number.

steps.label: TLB misses if the page size were 32 bytes instead
TLB misses at 16-byte pages if the array began at address 64

guided-practice.explain: One miss per distinct page touched, and every subsequent element on that page rides free: starting at 76 the array covers pages 4, 5, 6 and 7, so four misses. Doubling the page size halves the number of pages spanned, and moving the start to 64 aligns the array so it fits in three pages rather than straddling four - the same twelve accesses, one fewer miss, bought purely by alignment. The tempting count for the first step is three, from reasoning that twelve ints occupy 48 bytes and 48 bytes is three 16-byte pages; so they are, but only if they start on a page boundary.

guided-practice.prompt: A colleague objects that a 64-entry TLB covering an address space of a million pages is obviously hopeless, and that reported hit rates above 90% must be a measurement error. Explain why real programs achieve them anyway, naming the two forms of locality and saying what each one buys.
guided-practice.explain: The objection assumes accesses are spread uniformly over the address space, and they never are. Spatial locality means a single entry covers a whole page - four thousand bytes, a thousand ints - so one miss buys hundreds or thousands of hits from a sequential walk. Temporal locality means the handful of pages a loop actually uses, its code, its stack frame and its data, are re-referenced constantly and stay resident for the whole loop. The count that matters is not pages in the address space but pages in the working set, and that is usually small enough to fit - which is also why the hit rate collapses the moment a program's working set exceeds the TLB's reach.

tlb-drills.prompt: A fully associative TLB holds 4 entries and evicts the least recently used entry. Pages are 4 KB, the TLB starts empty and one process runs throughout. The following virtual addresses are accessed in order. For each, answer `hit` or `miss`.
tlb-drills.explain: Only the top 20 bits matter: 0x10000 and 0x10FFC are the same page 0x10, which is why the second access hits despite being 4092 bytes away - that is spatial locality made arithmetic. The interesting step is the seventh. Inserting page 0x14 into a full TLB evicts the least recently used entry, which by then is 0x11, so when 0x11008 arrives immediately afterwards it misses; page 0x10 survives because it was re-referenced at step six and is therefore the most recently used. Answering `hit` for the eighth access is the natural mistake - page 0x11 was loaded and nothing obviously removed it, but LRU removed it silently.

tlb-drills.prompt: A 32-bit machine uses 4 KB pages and a two-level page table split 10/10/12. The page directory's entry 1 points at a page table whose entry 2 holds frame 0x1F3 with the valid bit set. Directory entry 0 has its valid bit clear. Give the requested values for the virtual address 0x00402ABC, and then for 0x00000FFF. Write hexadecimal answers as `0x` followed by the digits, and `fault` where the access is illegal.
tlb-drills.explain: Shift right by 22 for the directory index, take the next ten bits for the table index, and copy the low twelve bits through untranslated - so the physical address ends in the same ABC the virtual address did, because a byte's position within a page never changes. The second address faults at the **first** level: directory entry 0 is invalid, so the entire lowest 4 MB of the address space has no page table at all and no second reference is even issued. That is the saving multi-level tables exist for, seen from the fault side - one invalid entry standing in for 1024 absent pages.

tlb-drills.prompt: Put the steps of a hardware-managed TLB miss into the order the hardware performs them, beginning from the arrival of a virtual address.
fragments: extract the VPN from the virtual address
search the TLB for that VPN and find no valid entry
read the page-table entry for that VPN from memory
check the PTE's valid bit and permissions
install the VPN-to-PFN mapping in the TLB
retry the instruction, which now hits in the TLB
tlb-drills.explain: The order that matters is the last two: the mapping is installed and the instruction is then restarted from the beginning, rather than the hardware finishing the access directly from the PTE it has just read. That restart is a deliberate simplification - there is exactly one path through translation, and the miss handler's only job is to make the fast path succeed next time. Checking permissions before installing also matters, since installing an entry for a page the process may not touch would cache a violation.

tlb-drills.prompt: A workload streams through a 4 MB buffer. Fill in the numbers for a 64-entry TLB. Give plain integers with no units.
tlb-drills.template:
reach with 4 KB pages          = ___ KB
pages needed to cover 4 MB     = ___
reach with 2 MB pages, in MB   = ___
tlb-drills.explain: Sixty-four entries at 4 KB reach 256 KB, but the buffer needs 1024 pages to describe it, so the TLB can hold one sixteenth of the mapping at a time and a single pass evicts what the next pass will want. Switching to 2 MB pages takes the reach to 128 MB, which covers the buffer thirty times over - the same hardware, the same program, and the miss rate falls to almost nothing. The number that catches people is the middle one: 4 MB divided by 4 KB is 1024, because the units differ by a factor of 1024, not by four.

table-design.prompt: A process on a 32-bit machine with 4 KB pages and 4-byte page-table entries uses 4 MB of code and heap at the very bottom of its address space and 8 KB of stack at the very top. Nothing else is mapped. Give each quantity as a plain integer.

steps.label: size in bytes of a linear (one-level) page table for this process
pages of memory that linear page table occupies
page-directory entries that must be valid under a two-level table
pages of memory the two-level structure occupies, including the directory
memory references a TLB miss costs under the two-level table, including the data fetch

table-design.explain: A linear table must describe all 2^20 pages whether they exist or not, so it is 4 MB and occupies 1024 pages of real memory to map a process that uses only 1026. Under two levels, one directory entry covers the bottom 4 MB and one covers the top 4 MB, and the 4088 MB of nothing in between costs 1022 invalid entries inside a page that had to be allocated anyway - so the whole structure is the directory plus two page tables, three pages, 12 KB. The price is on the miss path, where a directory read and a table read precede the data. The trap is answering 1 for the third step: the stack lives at the top of the address space, in a different 4 MB region entirely, and needs its own page table.

table-design.prompt: A numerical kernel walks a 1024 x 1024 array of 4-byte ints. Each row is exactly 4096 bytes, matching the machine's page size, and the CPU has a 64-entry TLB. Traversing the array row by row runs fast. The same loop with the two indices swapped, so that it walks down columns, runs many times slower, and the performance counters show a TLB miss on essentially every single access - just over a million of them. Memory bandwidth, cache size and the instruction count are unchanged. Name the cause and explain the mechanism.
table-design.answer: TLB thrashing: the column traversal's working set exceeds the TLB's reach
table-design.explain: Because a row is exactly one page, walking a column touches a different page at every step, with a stride of one whole page: the loop cycles through all 1024 pages, then begins the same cycle again for the next column. Sixty-four entries reach 256 KB, which is 64 of those 1024 pages, so by the time a page is wanted again it was evicted a thousand accesses ago and every one of the 1048576 accesses misses. The row-major version touches one new page per row - 1024 misses in total, a hit rate above 99.9% - because spatial locality is aligned with the traversal. The tempting diagnosis is the data cache, which is also thrashing here, but the counters name the TLB and the fixes differ: interchange the loops, block the traversal into tiles, or map the array with large pages so that 64 entries reach the whole 4 MB.

table-design.prompt: You are specifying the translation hardware and its operating-system support for a 32-bit embedded machine that runs a few dozen small processes and context-switches thousands of times a second. Argue for a TLB backed by a multi-level page table, and cover: what the TLB caches, and what a hit and a miss each cost in memory references; why a linear page table is unaffordable here, with worked numbers for 4 KB pages and 4-byte entries; how a two-level table exploits sparsity; why an inverted page table is a different trade and what it costs to search; why flushing the TLB on every switch would be ruinous at this switch rate and what address-space identifiers do instead; and the one invalidation the operating system must still perform by hand. There are no tests here: your answer is marked against a rubric of the points it must cover.
table-design.explain: The three decisions are separable and each has a number behind it. The TLB turns a hit back into a single memory reference and confines paging's extra references to the miss path. A linear table costs 4 MB per process - dozens of processes would need hundreds of megabytes before a single instruction ran - whereas a two-level table allocates a page table only for the 4 MB regions actually in use, typically three or four pages per process. An inverted table would be sized by physical memory rather than by process count, which is attractive on a small machine, but its index is by frame, so every translation becomes a hash lookup rather than an indexed read. Thousands of switches a second is exactly the regime where flushing is ruinous: every process would resume cold and re-miss its whole working set, so ASID tags are what reduce the switch to a register write - and even with them, unmapping a page or changing its permissions demands an explicit invalidation of that VPN, because the hardware never sees the page table change.

exam.prompt: What does a translation lookaside buffer hold?
choices: Recently used mappings from virtual page number to physical frame number, with protection and validity bits
The most recently accessed bytes of memory, so that repeated loads of the same address are fast
The page table of the currently running process, copied into the CPU at each context switch
A queue of pending page faults waiting for the operating system to service them
exam.explain: The TLB caches translations, not data - it is consulted before memory is touched, and on a hit exactly one memory reference is then made, for the datum itself. The second option describes the data cache, a different structure that sits after translation. The third is impossible for the very reason multi-level tables exist: a page table is megabytes, and no CPU could copy one on every switch.

exam.prompt: Which of these are true of an inverted page table? Select all that apply.
choices: It has one entry per physical frame rather than one per virtual page
A single table serves the whole machine rather than one per process
Each entry must record which process the frame currently belongs to
It removes the need for a TLB, because translation becomes a direct index
exam.explain: Indexing by frame is the defining inversion, and it is what makes one machine-wide table sufficient and its size a function of physical memory alone - but an entry then has to say whose virtual page it is holding, or the mapping means nothing. The final option reverses the consequence: inverting the index means a virtual address is no longer an index into anything, so a lookup becomes a search, usually through a hash table bolted alongside, and the TLB becomes more important rather than less.

exam.prompt: A fully associative TLB holds 3 entries and evicts the least recently used. Pages are 4 KB and the TLB starts empty. Answer `hit` or `miss` for each access in order.
exam.explain: After the fourth access the recency order is 0x41, 0x42, 0x40, so inserting 0x43 evicts 0x41 and the sixth access misses; page 0x40 survives to the end because it keeps being re-referenced. Answering `hit` at the sixth step is the natural error - the page was loaded and nothing obviously removed it, but LRU evicts the least recently **used**, not the least recently loaded, and 0x41 had not been touched since the second access.

exam.prompt: Processes A and B are interleaved on a machine with a 4-entry fully associative TLB using LRU. The access sequence, as (process, virtual page number), is: (A, 0x0A), (A, 0x0B), (B, 0x0A), (B, 0x0C), (A, 0x0A), (A, 0x0B), (B, 0x0A). The TLB starts empty. Compare a machine that flushes the whole TLB on every context switch with one whose entries carry address-space identifiers.

steps.label: hits out of 7, flushing on every switch
hits out of 7, with ASID-tagged entries
entries evicted for lack of space in the ASID case

exam.explain: Flushing gives seven misses out of seven: every switch empties the TLB, and because each process touches at most two pages before being switched away, no entry ever survives long enough to be reused. With ASIDs the four distinct (process, page) pairs fit exactly, so the last three accesses all hit and nothing is ever evicted for space - capacity was never the problem here, ownership was. The tempting answer for the first line is 1, from noticing that (A, 0x0B) follows (A, 0x0A) with no switch between them; but those are different pages, and 0x0B has not been seen before.

exam.prompt: Fill in the sizes for a 32-bit address space with 4 KB pages and 4-byte page-table entries. Give plain integers.
exam.template:
pages in the address space                    = 2^___
bytes in a linear page table                 = ___ MB
entries in a 4 KB page directory             = ___
address space one valid directory entry covers = ___ MB
exam.explain: Thirty-two address bits minus twelve offset bits leaves twenty bits of page number, so 2^20 pages at 4 bytes each is 4 MB. A directory is itself one page, and 4096 bytes of 4-byte entries is 1024 of them - which is also how many pages one page table maps, so each directory entry stands for 1024 x 4 KB, or 4 MB. That both numbers come out as '4' is a coincidence of this particular split, and worth deriving rather than memorising, because a machine with 8 KB pages gives different answers throughout.

exam.prompt: Put these in order of increasing cost in memory references for one data access on a machine with 4 KB pages, cheapest first.
fragments: TLB hit
TLB miss with a linear page table
TLB miss with a two-level page table
TLB miss with a four-level page table
exam.explain: One reference, then two, three and five: each level of table adds one read to the miss path, and the data fetch is always the last one. The ordering is the whole argument of this floor in miniature - deeper tables are how the space cost of paging is paid down, and the TLB is what makes their extra references rare enough to accept.

exam.prompt: On a 32-bit machine with a 10/10/12 split, give the page-directory index in decimal for each virtual address.
exam.explain: Shifting right by 22 bits is the same as asking which 4 MB region the address lies in: 0x7FE00000 is 2046 MB, and 2046 divided by 4 is 511. Working digit by digit in hexadecimal invites error because a 22-bit shift cuts a hex digit in half; converting to megabytes and dividing by four is both faster and harder to get wrong.

exam.prompt: Explain how a two-level page table can map the same address space as a linear one while using a small fraction of the memory, and state precisely what the arrangement costs. Refer to what makes an address space sparse and to what happens on a TLB miss.
exam.explain: A linear table pays for every page of the address space whether it exists or not, and almost none of it does - a process's code, heap and stack occupy a few regions with an enormous invalid hole between them. Chopping the table into page-sized pieces and adding a directory above it means a piece describing only absent pages is never allocated at all, so the structure grows with what is used rather than with what could be addressed. The cost is one extra memory reference per level on the miss path, and that is acceptable only because the TLB makes misses rare; without it, deeper tables would simply multiply the price of every access.

exam.prompt: A database keeps a 6 GB in-memory index and touches it in an essentially random pattern. The machine's TLB has 1536 entries and the pages are 4 KB. Profiling shows the CPU spending a large fraction of its cycles on page-table walks even though the index is entirely resident in RAM and no page faults occur. Recommend a change, justify it with the arithmetic of TLB reach, and say honestly what your recommendation costs.
exam.explain: The reach is 1536 x 4 KB, which is 6 MB - one thousandth of the index - and a random access pattern gives the TLB no locality to exploit, so nearly every access pays a full page-table walk while never faulting, exactly the symptom described. Mapping the index with 2 MB large pages raises the reach to 3 GB and brings most of the working set inside it. The costs are real and should be stated: large pages waste memory internally when a region is not a multiple of 2 MB, they need contiguous physical memory that a fragmented system may be unable to supply, and they make the granularity of paging, protection and copy-on-write far coarser. Adding RAM or a faster disc would change nothing here, because nothing was ever waiting on either.

sections.title: One more bit, and memory stops being a limit
sections.body:
Every mechanism so far has assumed the address space fits in RAM. Drop that assumption and the address space becomes what it always pretended to be: a description of memory the process **might** touch, backed wherever the operating system finds convenient. The kernel reserves a region of disk - **swap space** - and treats physical frames as a cache over it.

The entire trick is one bit in the page-table entry. The **present bit** says whether this page is currently in a frame. If it is clear, the frame-number field is free to mean something else entirely: which swap slot holds the page. Hardware that finds a valid page with `present == 0` raises a **page fault** and hands control to the kernel, which is the only party that knows what disks are.

Note what is **not** happening here. A page fault is not an error, and it is not the same event as an invalid access: `valid == 0` means the page was never part of the address space and the process is buggy, while `present == 0` means the page is real and simply elsewhere. Conflating the two is the commonest confusion in this material, and the two bits exist precisely to keep them apart.

The fault path is then mechanical: read the swap slot out of the entry, obtain a free frame - possibly by evicting somebody, which is the next three sections - issue the disk read, block the faulting process while the disk works, update the page-table entry and the TLB, and **retry the instruction**. Because the instruction restarts rather than resumes, the process sees only a delay. A very large delay: a memory reference costs about 100 ns and a disk read about 10 ms, five orders of magnitude apart, which is why **demand paging** - fetch a page only when it is actually referenced - is worth the complexity. Pages never touched are never read.

annotations.text: The same 20 bits mean a frame number when present is 1 and a swap slot when it is 0. Nothing else in the entry has to change for a page to move to disk and back.
This is the invalid case, not the fault case. It ends in a signal because the address space never contained this page; a present-bit fault ends in a disk read because it did.
Blocking here is the whole cost. The process is descheduled and the CPU runs somebody else, which is why demand paging degrades throughput gracefully - until it does not.
Retry, exactly as on a TLB miss: the instruction runs again from the beginning and this time the hardware finds the page present.

checkpoint.prompt: A process touches a page whose entry has `valid == 1` and `present == 0`. Put the steps that follow into the order they happen.
fragments: hardware walks the page table, finds present == 0 and raises a page fault
the kernel's fault handler reads the swap slot number out of the entry
the kernel finds a free frame, running the replacement policy if none is free
the disk read is issued and the faulting process blocks
the entry's frame number and present bit are updated and the TLB is filled
the faulting instruction is retried and completes
checkpoint.explain: The free frame must be found before the read is issued, because the read needs somewhere to land - and finding it may itself require evicting and writing back another page. The tempting reordering is to put the TLB fill after the retry, but the retry only succeeds because the entry and the TLB already describe a present page.

sections.title: Choosing a victim: the perfect policy and the naive one
sections.body:
Once frames are a cache, every miss is a **replacement** decision, and the cost model is brutal. With a memory reference at $T_M = 100$ ns and a disk access at $T_D = 10$ ms, the average time is $AMAT = (1 - P_{miss}) \cdot T_M + P_{miss} \cdot T_D$. At a 90% hit rate that is about 1 ms per access - ten thousand times slower than memory. At 99.9% it is about 10 µs, still a hundredfold slowdown. Hit rates that would delight a cache designer are catastrophic here, so a policy is judged on the misses it avoids, not the hits it scores.

The baseline is **OPT**: evict the page that will be referenced furthest in the future. It provably minimises faults, and it is unimplementable, because it requires knowing the future. That is not a defect - it is the point. OPT exists to tell you how much of a policy's fault count is the workload's doing and how much is the policy's.

**FIFO** is the naive answer: a queue of arrivals, evict the head. It costs nothing on a hit, and that is exactly what is wrong with it - a page referenced on every single access is evicted the moment it reaches the front, because FIFO never learns that it is hot. On the reference string `0 1 2 0 1 3 0 3 1 2 1` with three frames, OPT takes 5 faults and FIFO takes 7.

FIFO also has a property no sane policy should have. Give it **more memory and it can fault more**: on `1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5`, FIFO takes 9 faults with three frames and 10 with four. This is **Belady's anomaly**. It happens because FIFO's contents are not a **stack**: the set of pages held with three frames is not guaranteed to be a subset of the set held with four, so a larger cache can hold a genuinely different and worse collection. LRU and OPT are stack policies and cannot do this - LRU takes 10 faults on that string with three frames and 8 with four, monotonically better.

annotations.text: The hit path does nothing. That single omission is the whole difference between FIFO and LRU, and the entire reason FIFO evicts hot pages.
Oldest arrival, not least useful. The queue records when a page came in and never records that it has been wanted a thousand times since.
Verified by simulation, not by intuition: four frames really is worse here. Any argument that more cache must mean fewer misses is assuming the stack property, which FIFO does not have.

checkpoint.prompt: Run **FIFO** with 3 frames over `0 1 2 0 1 3 0 3 1 2 1`, starting empty. Give the running total of page faults after each reference listed.
checkpoint.explain: Reference 6 evicts page 0 - the oldest arrival - even though it was touched only two references earlier, so reference 7 faults on a page that was resident moments before. Answering 5 at the end is the usual slip: 5 is OPT's and LRU's count on this string, and the gap of two is precisely what FIFO's empty hit path costs.

sections.title: LRU, and why the real system approximates it
sections.body:
**LRU** evicts the page least recently used, betting that the recent past predicts the near future. On real workloads that bet pays: programs have temporal locality, and LRU on `0 1 2 0 1 3 0 3 1 2 1` matches OPT exactly at 5 faults. It is also a stack policy, so more memory never hurts it.

The problem is not the idea, it is the accounting. Exact LRU means updating a timestamp or a list position on **every memory reference** - not every fault, every reference. That is hardware work on the fast path, and then eviction has to scan every frame to find the minimum. On a machine with four million frames, doing that per fault is absurd. A policy that is a few per cent better and a hundred times more expensive to consult is not better.

So the hardware provides one bit instead of a clock value: the **reference bit**, set on every access and cleared only by the kernel. It cannot tell you **when** a page was used, only whether it has been used since you last looked - and that turns out to be enough. The **clock algorithm** sweeps a hand round the frames: a page with its reference bit set gets a second chance, the bit is cleared and the hand moves on; the first page found with the bit already clear is the victim. Pages in active use keep resetting their own bit and are never caught; a page nobody wants sits with a clear bit and is taken on the next sweep.

Clock is not LRU and does not claim to be - it distinguishes **used recently** from **not used recently** and no more, so it can evict a page more recently touched than one it spares. It costs one bit per frame and no work at all on a hit. The **dirty bit** refines it further: a clean victim costs one disk read to replace, a dirty one costs a write **and** a read, so a sweep may prefer clean pages. And when locality is absent - a loop over 5 pages in 4 frames - LRU and clock and FIFO all achieve a 0% hit rate, evicting each page exactly one reference before it is wanted, while **random** would get some of them by luck. There is no policy that beats a workload with no locality; there are only policies that fail less absurdly.

annotations.text: One integer for the entire policy. Compare with exact LRU, which needs a per-frame timestamp updated by hardware on every load and store.
A clear bit is the only evidence clock ever uses: this page has not been touched since the hand last passed. It says nothing about how long ago that was.

Clearing the bit is what makes the sweep terminate. If every frame is referenced, the first pass clears every bit and the second pass evicts the frame the hand started on - degenerating to FIFO, which is the sensible fallback.
Two I/Os against one. On a fault the process is already blocked, so halving the I/O on the critical path is worth passing over a slightly colder victim.

checkpoint.prompt: Three frames, clock replacement, hand starting at frame 0, all frames empty and filled left to right. Reference string `0 1 2 0 3 1 4 2 0 3`. For each reference below give the page **evicted**, or `hit`, or `none` if it filled an empty frame.
checkpoint.explain: At reference 5 every bit is set, so the hand clears all three and evicts the page in the frame it started on. At reference 7 the hand stands on page 1, whose bit was re-set by reference 6, so page 1 gets its second chance and page 2 is taken instead - even though page 2 was referenced more recently than page 3. Expecting LRU's victim is the natural error: clock only ever sees one bit.

sections.title: When there is not enough memory at all
sections.body:
Every policy above assumes the pages a process actually needs will mostly fit. When they do not, the machine **thrashes**: each fault evicts a page that is about to be referenced, so the next reference faults, and the system spends its time moving pages rather than running instructions. The signature is unmistakable and counter-intuitive - CPU utilisation near zero, disk utilisation near 100%, and admitting more processes makes it worse. A scheduler that reads low CPU utilisation as **idle** and admits more work drives the machine straight off the cliff.

Denning's answer names the quantity that matters. The **working set** $WS(t, \Delta)$ is the set of distinct pages referenced in the last $\Delta$ references; its size is how much memory the process needs **right now** in order to run without thrashing. The sum of the working sets over runnable processes is the machine's true demand. If that sum exceeds the number of frames, no replacement policy can save you, because the deficit is arithmetic and not a matter of choosing better victims.

What does help is **admission control**: refuse to run everything at once. Suspend a process entirely, swap its pages out, and give the rest enough frames to hold their working sets; run the suspended one later when memory frees up. This is the honest response - a smaller number of processes making progress beats all of them making none. Modern Linux mostly declines to do it and invokes the out-of-memory killer instead, which is a blunter version of the same admission decision.

The last lever is to stop paying one fault per page. **Prefetching** exploits the fact that the expensive part of a disk access is getting there: having sought to a swap slot, reading its neighbours costs almost nothing extra. So the kernel **clusters** - grouping swap writes so related pages land together, then reading a run of them per fault. Prefetching is a bet on spatial locality, and like every bet it is sometimes wrong: a wrong guess wastes bandwidth and, worse, a frame that something else wanted.

annotations.text: D is a window over references, not over seconds. That is what makes the working set a property of the program's behaviour rather than of the machine's speed.
Summing working sets, not address-space sizes. A process with a 4 GB address space and a 12 MB working set costs the machine 12 MB.
Suspending one process is the only move that actually reduces demand. Every alternative - a cleverer victim, a bigger swap file - redistributes a deficit that arithmetic says cannot be met.
The seek dominates, so the second, third and fourth pages of a cluster are nearly free. That asymmetry is the whole justification for guessing.

checkpoint.prompt: Complete the description of a thrashing machine and of the quantity that predicts it.
checkpoint.template:
A thrashing system shows CPU utilisation near ___ and disk utilisation near ___.
The set of distinct pages a process referenced in its last D references is its ___ ___.
When the sum of those over runnable processes exceeds the number of frames, the only real fix is to ___ a process.
checkpoint.explain: The utilisation figures are the diagnostic that matters, because they are the pair that misleads: a nearly idle CPU normally means admit more work, and here it means exactly the opposite. The fix is subtractive because the deficit is arithmetic - the frames demanded exceed the frames that exist, and no ordering of victims changes that sum.

guided-practice.prompt: Put the events of a page fault on a page that currently lives in swap into the order the machine performs them.
fragments: the MMU finds valid == 1, present == 0 and traps to the kernel
the kernel decides which resident page to evict, since no frame is free
the victim is written back to swap, but only if its dirty bit is set
the faulting page is read from its swap slot into the freed frame
the page-table entry is rewritten with the new frame and present == 1
the instruction that faulted is retried from the beginning
guided-practice.explain: The write-back sits between choosing the victim and reading the new page, and it happens only for a dirty victim - a clean page already has an identical copy in swap, so overwriting its frame loses nothing. Putting the read before the eviction is the tempting order, but the read needs a frame to land in and there is none until the victim leaves.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete the two bits that separate a real bug from an ordinary fault, and the two the replacement policy consults.
guided-practice.template:
valid == 0 means the page was never mapped, so the kernel sends ___ .
present == 0 with valid == 1 means the page is in ___ space and must be read back.
The bit hardware sets on every access, and the kernel clears, is the ___ bit.
The bit that decides whether an eviction costs one disk I/O or two is the ___ bit.
guided-practice.explain: Two bits are needed because two different things can be wrong with an address and only one of them is the process's fault. The reference bit is an approximation of recency and the dirty bit is a statement about cost - confusing them leads to the idea that clock spares dirty pages for recency reasons, when the reason is purely the extra write.

guided-practice.prompt: Run **LRU** with 3 frames over `0 1 2 0 1 3 0 3 1 2 1`, starting empty. Give the running total of page faults after each reference listed.
guided-practice.explain: At reference 6 LRU evicts page 2, untouched since reference 3, so pages 0 and 1 both survive and reference 7 hits - exactly where FIFO faulted. The one fault LRU cannot avoid is at reference 10, and OPT cannot avoid it either: five is the best any policy achieves on this string.

guided-practice.prompt: Run **OPT** with 3 frames over `0 1 2 0 1 3 0 3 1 2 1`, starting empty. At each fault listed give the page it evicts, or `none` if a frame was free.
guided-practice.explain: At reference 6 the resident pages 0, 1 and 2 are next needed at references 7, 9 and 10, so page 2 is furthest away and goes. At reference 10, page 0 is never referenced again at all, which is as far in the future as a page can be. OPT's count is the floor: if a policy beats 5 here, the simulation is wrong.

policy-traces.prompt: Reference string `1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5`, starting empty. Run **FIFO** twice - once with 3 frames, once with 4 - and report the figures below.

steps.label: 3 frames: page evicted when 5 is first referenced
4 frames: page evicted when 5 is first referenced
4 frames: does the final reference to 5 hit or fault?

policy-traces.explain: With three frames the early churn happens to leave 1 and 2 resident when they are next wanted, and 5 survives to the end, so three references hit. With four frames the hits come earlier - 1 and 2 at references 5 and 6 - and every page is then evicted just before its next use, so only two hit in total. More memory produced more faults; that is Belady's anomaly, and it is possible because FIFO's three-frame contents are not a subset of its four-frame contents. Expecting four frames to be weakly better is the reflex to unlearn: that guarantee comes from the stack property, which FIFO lacks.

policy-traces.prompt: Same string, `1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5`, starting empty. Now run **LRU** and **OPT** at both frame counts and report the fault totals.

steps.label: At 3 frames, which faults more - FIFO or LRU?

policy-traces.explain: Both LRU and OPT improve when given a fourth frame, as stack policies must: their k-frame contents are always a subset of their (k+1)-frame contents, so every hit at the smaller size is still a hit at the larger one. The surprise is the last step - on this particular string LRU is worse than FIFO at three frames. Belady's anomaly is about one policy compared with itself at two sizes, not about one policy always beating another, and those two claims are easy to conflate.

policy-traces.prompt: Three frames, **clock** replacement, hand starting at frame 0, all frames empty and filled left to right. Reference string `0 1 2 0 3 1 4 2 0 3`. Give the page evicted at each reference below, and the total faults.
policy-traces.explain: Twice the hand spares a page LRU would have taken and takes one LRU would have kept: at reference 7, page 1 had its bit re-set by the reference before, so page 2 goes instead. Exact LRU faults nine times on this string and clock faults eight, which is a useful corrective - an approximation is not systematically worse, it is merely different, and on any given string either can win.

policy-traces.prompt: A process makes the references `2 6 1 5 7 7 7 7 5 1 6 2 3 4 1 2 3 4 4 4 3 4 4 4 1 1 1` at positions 1 to 27. With a working-set window of $\Delta = 10$, give $|WS(t, 10)|$ at each position below.
policy-traces.explain: The window at t = 14 straddles two phases - the tail of the 5/6/7 locality and the head of the 1/2/3/4 one - so it names seven pages the process does not simultaneously need, which is exactly why the working set peaks at a phase change and then subsides. A machine with six frames runs this process happily up to t = 13 and again from t = 18 onwards, and thrashes in between; sizing memory to the average rather than the peak is how that transient becomes a stall.

policy-traces.prompt: A numerical kernel walks the same 5-page array over and over. Given 4 frames it measures a hit rate of exactly 0% - every single reference faults - under LRU, and again under clock. The engineer concludes the LRU implementation is broken. Name the real cause, and explain why switching to **random** replacement measurably improves the hit rate.
policy-traces.answer: A cyclic reference pattern one page larger than the cache, so LRU evicts each page exactly one reference before it is next needed
policy-traces.explain: LRU is behaving perfectly; the workload is adversarial to it. In a cycle of 5 pages through 4 frames the least recently used page is always the one about to be referenced, so LRU's rule picks the worst possible victim every time - and clock, sweeping frames whose bits are all set, degenerates to the same order. Random has no rule to exploit, so it keeps some pages by luck and scores a non-zero hit rate: one of the few cases where knowing nothing beats knowing the recent past.

memory-pressure.prompt: A batch server runs 12 jobs. Monitoring shows CPU utilisation at 3%, the swap device 99% busy, and job completion times an order of magnitude above normal. The operator, seeing an idle CPU, starts four more jobs; everything gets dramatically worse. Name the condition, explain what the extra jobs did, and say what should be done instead.
memory-pressure.answer: Thrashing - the combined working sets exceed physical memory, and admitting more processes deepens the deficit
memory-pressure.explain: The 3% figure is not idleness, it is the CPU waiting on a disk every process is queued behind - the one situation where low utilisation means the machine is over-subscribed rather than under-used. Each new job needs its own working set of frames, taken from processes that were already short, so the fault rate climbs and the CPU falls further. The only move that reduces demand is subtractive: suspend processes until the surviving working sets fit in the frames that exist.

memory-pressure.prompt: A colleague configures a fleet of servers with zero swap space, arguing that swapping is slow so removing it removes the slowness, and that RAM is cheap anyway. Assess this. What behaviour does the machine lose, what does it gain, and what happens now when memory is over-committed?
memory-pressure.explain: With no swap the kernel loses the ability to evict anonymous pages - heap and stack, which have nowhere else to live - so under pressure it can only reclaim clean file-backed pages and re-read them from the filesystem on the next fault. Demand paging itself is untouched, because executables and mapped files still page in on a present-bit fault from their own files. What is gained is a bound on tail latency; what is lost is the graceful middle, so over-commitment stops meaning slow and starts meaning the out-of-memory killer picks a process to destroy.

memory-pressure.prompt: Exact LRU is not implemented in any general-purpose operating system, yet clock - a cruder approximation of it - is everywhere. Explain what makes exact LRU unaffordable, and what clock gives up in exchange for being affordable.
memory-pressure.explain: The cost is not in the eviction, it is in the bookkeeping: exact LRU must update per-page recency on every memory reference, on the hardware fast path, and then scan every frame to find the minimum - work proportional to physical memory on each fault. Clock replaces the recency value with a single hardware-set reference bit and the scan with a hand that stops at the first clear one, so it does nothing at all on a hit. What it gives up is ordering: it can say used-since-last-sweep or not, and nothing finer, so it will sometimes evict a page touched more recently than one it spares.

memory-pressure.prompt: Design the replacement and fetch policy for a kernel whose swap device is a fast SSD with expensive writes: a read costs 100 µs, a write costs 800 µs and wears the device. You have per-frame reference and dirty bits and a background thread you may use. Describe victim selection, how the dirty bit changes it, what you prefetch and on what evidence, and how the kernel detects that no choice of victim can help.
memory-pressure.explain: The asymmetry is the whole design: a clean victim costs one read on the fault path and a dirty one costs a write plus a read, so the sweep should prefer clean frames while a background thread writes dirty pages back early, converting them to clean before the hand arrives - which also spreads the writes out instead of bursting them onto the critical path. Prefetching is a weaker bet on an SSD than on a disk, because there is no seek to amortise, so it should follow observed sequential access rather than being applied always. And no arrangement of victims fixes a working-set sum larger than the frame count, so the design must include the fault-rate threshold at which it stops choosing victims and starts suspending processes.

exam.prompt: What does the **present bit** in a page-table entry indicate?
choices: That the page has been written to since it was last paged in
That the page currently occupies a physical frame rather than living in swap
That the page is part of this process's address space at all
That the page has been referenced since the kernel last cleared the bit
exam.explain: The other three describe the dirty bit, the valid bit and the reference bit respectively. The pairing that matters is present with valid: valid says whether the page exists in the address space, present says whether it happens to be in RAM right now, and only the second of those can be false without the process being buggy.

exam.prompt: Which of the following are true of **OPT**, the optimal replacement policy?
choices: It evicts the page whose next reference is furthest in the future
It provably minimises the number of page faults for a given reference string
It can be implemented if the kernel keeps a long enough reference history
It is a stack policy, so more frames never increase its fault count
It is used in production kernels for read-only pages
exam.explain: OPT needs the future, and no length of history supplies it - the third option tempts because recency-based policies really are built from history, but they approximate OPT rather than achieving it. The fourth is true and often overlooked: OPT is a stack policy, which is why it serves as a well-behaved baseline against which FIFO's anomaly stands out.

exam.prompt: Complete the average-access-time model for demand paging. Give the third blank in nanoseconds and the fourth as a whole number.
exam.template:
AMAT = (1 - Pmiss) * ___ + Pmiss * ___
With a memory access of 100 ns and a disk access of 10 ms, a 99% hit rate gives an AMAT of ___ ns.
That is roughly a ___-fold slowdown against memory speed.
exam.explain: 0.99 x 100 + 0.01 x 10,000,000 = 99 + 100,000 = 100,099 ns, and dividing by the 100 ns baseline gives about 1001. The lesson buried in the arithmetic is that the miss term swamps the hit term at any hit rate a cache designer would call good, which is why paging systems chase the last fraction of a per cent.

exam.prompt: Order these three policies by the number of faults they take on `1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5` with **3 frames**, fewest faults first.
fragments: OPT
FIFO
LRU
exam.explain: OPT takes 7, FIFO 9 and LRU 10. OPT is first by definition, but the order of the other two is the point: LRU loses to FIFO on this string. A policy's average advantage over real workloads is not a guarantee on any particular one, and a benchmark of a single reference string proves nothing about either.

exam.prompt: Three frames, **FIFO**, starting empty. Reference string `7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4 2 3 0 3 2`. Give the running fault total after each reference listed.
exam.explain: Reference 5 hits because page 0 is still in the queue, but reference 6 evicts it anyway - FIFO's queue position never moved when it hit. Only the last two references hit after that, which is why the total sits at 10 out of 13; LRU takes 9 and OPT takes 7 on the same string.

exam.prompt: Three frames, **clock**, hand starting at frame 0, all frames empty and filled left to right. Reference string `1 2 3 1 4 1 5 2 1 3`. Give the page evicted at each reference below, and the total faults.
exam.explain: Every frame's bit is set when reference 5 arrives, so the hand clears all three and evicts the page in the frame it started on - page 1, which had just been referenced. That is clock at its most FIFO-like, and it is why it takes 8 faults here where LRU takes 7: with every bit set the one bit carries no information, and the sweep falls back to position.

exam.prompt: Belady's anomaly is often stated as 'more memory can mean more faults'. Explain the property FIFO lacks that permits this, and why LRU and OPT are immune to it.
