exam.explain: A stack policy guarantees that the set of pages held with k frames is always a subset of the set held with k+1 frames, so every hit at the smaller size is still a hit at the larger one and the fault count can only fall. LRU and OPT satisfy this because their victim depends on the reference string alone - the k most recently used pages are a subset of the k+1 most recently used - while FIFO's victim depends on arrival order, which a different frame count changes, so the two configurations drift into genuinely different and incomparable contents.

exam.prompt: A service is fast for hours, then a nightly report starts and every request slows by 50x while the swap device saturates. When the report finishes, speed returns without a restart. The service's own resident set never grew. Name the cause and explain why the service degraded even though its own memory demand never changed.
exam.answer: Global replacement under memory over-commitment - the report's working set pushes the machine's total demand past the frame count, so the service's pages are evicted and it thrashes
exam.explain: Replacement is global: the policy chooses victims from all frames, so a newcomer with a large working set takes frames from an innocent neighbour rather than from itself. The service's demand was constant and its supply collapsed, which is why nothing in its own metrics explains the slowdown and why it recovers by itself the moment the report exits. Per-process frame allocation, or a working-set-based admission rule, would have contained the damage to the report.

sections.title: One address space, many stacks
sections.body:
A process is two things bundled together: an address space, and a thread of control running through it. **Threads** take that bundle apart. Creating a second thread inside a process gives you a second program counter and a second set of registers running through the **same** address space - the same code, the same globals, the same heap, the same open files.

Only two things are private. Each thread gets its own **stack**, so that its local variables and its chain of return addresses do not collide with anyone else's; and each thread gets its own register state, saved and restored on a context switch exactly as a process's is. Everything else is common property, which is why an address space with threads in it is drawn with several stacks scattered through the middle of it rather than one tidy stack at the top.

The reason to want this is parallelism and overlap. Two threads on two cores work on one data set without the copying, the marshalling and the explicit messages that two processes would need, and a thread that blocks on a slow disk read does not stop the others. A context switch between threads of the same process is cheaper too, because the address space does not change: the page table stays put and the TLB need not be flushed.

And that shared address space is the whole bill, paid at once. Two processes that both hold a variable called `counter` hold two different variables and cannot possibly interfere. Two threads that both hold `counter` hold **one** variable, and the scheduler may switch between them at any instruction boundary it likes. What was structurally impossible has become the default hazard.

annotations.text: One `counter`, at one address, for the whole process. Two processes doing this would have two counters and no problem at all.
`i` lives on the calling thread's own stack, so each thread has its own. This is the line nobody worries about, and it is the only one that is genuinely safe.
Six increments are issued in total. The final value is anywhere from 2 to 6, and which one you get depends on where the timer interrupt happens to land.
`pthread_join` is the only synchronisation in this program. It orders the end of the threads against `main`, and orders nothing at all between the threads themselves.

checkpoint.prompt: For each part of a multi-threaded process, write exactly `shared` if all threads see one copy, or `private` if every thread has its own.
checkpoint.template:
code (text) segment: ___
global variables: ___
the heap: ___
the stack: ___
the register set and program counter: ___
the file descriptor table: ___
checkpoint.explain: Only the stack and the register state are per-thread, and they are per-thread for the same reason: they record where a particular thread is in its own execution, which no other thread has any business overwriting. Everything reachable through the address space - globals, heap, code - is one copy. The file descriptor table catches people out because it feels like an execution detail, but it belongs to the process, which is why one thread closing a descriptor closes it for all of them.

sections.title: The race, one instruction at a time
sections.body:
`counter = counter + 1` looks indivisible because it is one line. The processor does not see lines. It sees a **load** that copies the value out of memory into a register, an **add** that changes the register while memory sits untouched, and a **store** that writes the register back - and a timer interrupt may land in either of the two gaps.

When it does, the interrupted thread's register is saved into its context and the other thread runs. If that other thread loads the same variable, it loads the value that is still in memory - the **stale** one, because the first thread's update is sitting in a saved register where nobody can see it. Both threads then compute the same new value and both store it. Two increments happened; the variable moved by one. This is a **lost update**, and it is the canonical shape of a **race condition**: a result that depends on the order in which threads happened to be scheduled.

The damage is not bounded by one. With two threads each incrementing a counter a thousand times, the maximum is the 2000 you expected and the minimum is **2** - and every value in between is reachable by some schedule. The counter is not merely a little bit wrong; the answer carries no information about how much work was done.

What makes races unpleasant to hunt is that the buggy schedules are rare. The window between the load and the store is a few nanoseconds wide, so the program passes its tests, passes review, and corrupts data in production under load or on a machine with more cores. A test that passes tells you nothing here: you have not shown the race cannot happen, only that this particular run did not hit it.
sections.code:
/* One line of C. Three instructions, and the timer interrupt may land
   between any two of them:

       mov 0x8049a1c, %eax      LOAD  : counter -> register
       add $0x1, %eax           ADD   : register + 1; memory untouched
       mov %eax, 0x8049a1c      STORE : register -> counter               */

counter = counter + 1;

/* An interleaving that loses an update. counter starts at 50.

   Thread 1        Thread 2        counter   T1.eax   T2.eax
   ---------------------------------------------------------
   LOAD                              50        50       -
   ADD                               50        51       -
   -- interrupt: T1's registers are saved into its context --
                   LOAD              50        51       50
                   ADD               50        51       51
                   STORE             51        51       51
   -- interrupt: T2's context saved, T1's eax restored to 51 --
   STORE                             51        51       51

   Two increments ran to completion. counter went from 50 to 51.        */

annotations.text: The add touches only the register. Between this instruction and the store, the new value exists nowhere that another thread can see.
One line of source, and the source is what misleads you. Nothing in C promises that a statement is indivisible.
T2 loads 50, not 51, because 51 exists only in T1's saved register. This single line is the whole bug.
T1's store overwrites T2's identical result with the same number, which is why nothing looks corrupted afterwards - the value is simply too small.

checkpoint.prompt: `counter` starts at 7. Two threads each run one `counter = counter + 1`, decomposed into LOAD, ADD, STORE. The schedule is: T1 LOAD, T1 ADD, [switch], T2 LOAD, T2 ADD, T2 STORE, [switch], T1 STORE. Give the value of `counter` in memory after each of the six instructions.
checkpoint.explain: Memory changes on stores and on nothing else, so four of the six steps leave `counter` exactly where it was. The instructive step is T2's LOAD: it reads 7, not 8, because T1's 8 is in a saved register rather than in memory. Both stores therefore write 8, and two increments move the counter by one.

sections.title: What a lock must promise
sections.body:
The region of code that must not be interleaved - here, the three instructions of the increment - is a **critical section**. What we need over it is **mutual exclusion**: a guarantee that at most one thread is inside at a time, so that the section behaves as though it were a single indivisible step. That property is **atomicity**, and since the hardware refuses to give it to us for arbitrary code, we build it.

A **lock** is the tool. It is an ordinary variable holding the state of the region - free, or held by someone - with `lock()` at the entry and `unlock()` at the exit. `lock()` returns only when the caller owns the region; every other thread reaching the entry waits. Note what the lock does **not** do: it puts no order on the threads, so it does not make the program deterministic. It only guarantees that whatever order occurs, one thread finishes the section before the next begins.

Judge any lock on three things. **Correctness** - does it actually exclude, on every schedule and on every core? **Fairness** - does every waiting thread eventually get in, or can one starve while others repeatedly overtake it? **Performance** - what does it cost when uncontended, when contended on one core, and when contended across many? These pull against each other, which is why there is more than one lock in the world.

The cheapest idea is to remove the thing that causes interleaving: switch interrupts off around the section, as in the second function below. On a single processor this genuinely works, and the kernel does use it in short, internal, interrupt-related places. As a general facility it fails on every count. It needs a privileged instruction, so it cannot be handed to user code - a thread that masked interrupts and looped would own the machine. It hides too much: a lost timer tick, a missed disk completion, a long critical section that delays every device on the machine. And on a multiprocessor it does not even work, because masking interrupts on **this** core says nothing about the thread running on the one next to it.

annotations.text: The entry point. Every path into the critical section must go through it, including the error paths - one early `return` that skips the unlock is a deadlock waiting for its first contended run.

The critical section is the data's invariant, not a line count. Anything that must not be seen half-done belongs inside; anything that need not be belongs outside, where it does not cost other threads their turn.
On a multiprocessor this function excludes nobody. The thread on the next core never wanted an interrupt in order to run.
This is a privileged instruction. Handing it to user code hands over the machine, which is the first of three reasons interrupt masking is not a general lock.

checkpoint.prompt: A colleague proposes replacing every `pthread_mutex_lock` in a user-space server with a pair of calls that disable and re-enable interrupts, arguing that it is faster because it never blocks. Give the reasons this cannot be adopted.
checkpoint.explain: Three separate objections, and the fatal one is the last. Disabling interrupts is privileged, so a user-space server cannot execute it at all; if it could, a thread that masked and then looped would monopolise the processor with no timer left to preempt it; and even in the kernel it excludes only the threads on this core, so on any multiprocessor the thread running beside you walks straight into the critical section. The tempting reading is that it is a fast lock with awkward permissions, but on more than one core it is not a lock at all.

sections.title: Building a lock from one atomic instruction
sections.body:
You cannot build mutual exclusion out of ordinary loads and stores at reasonable cost, because the test of the flag and the setting of the flag are themselves two instructions with a gap between them - the very problem we are trying to solve, moved one level down. Hardware breaks the regress by providing a single instruction that does both: **test-and-set** returns the old value of a word and writes a new one, indivisibly.

That is enough for a lock. `lock()` spins calling test-and-set with 1. If it gets 0 back, the flag was free and this thread has just taken it - and no other thread can have taken it too, because only one call can be the one that saw 0. If it gets 1 back it has changed nothing that matters and simply tries again. This **spin lock** is correct and tiny. It is not fair - a waiting thread has no queue position and may be overtaken indefinitely - and on a single processor it is close to the worst thing you could do, since a spinner burns its entire quantum waiting for a holder that cannot run until the spinner is preempted.

**Compare-and-swap** is the more general primitive: it writes only if the word still holds the value you expected, and returns what it actually found. Used as a lock it behaves exactly like test-and-set. Used directly it does more, because the return value tells the thread whether its whole read-modify-write was based on stale data, so it can retry the update rather than hold a lock at all. That is the basis of lock-free structures - and note that retrying is not free either, since under heavy contention threads can spend most of their time losing races.

The last decision is **granularity**: how much data one lock protects. A single lock over a whole hash table is trivially correct and trivially serialising - it makes the table a one-thread-at-a-time object, and the ceiling on throughput is one critical section after another however many cores you own. One lock per bucket lets threads touching different buckets proceed together and multiplies that ceiling, at the cost of more memory, more acquisitions per operation, and the real hazard: any operation touching two buckets now takes two locks, and two threads taking them in opposite orders will deadlock. Coarse locks are slow and safe; fine locks are fast and easy to get wrong.

annotations.text: These three lines are the whole point, and they are not three lines in hardware. Written as C they would themselves race; as one instruction they cannot.
Getting 0 back means the flag was free and you are the one who took it. The return value is the proof of ownership - which is why a plain store could never do this job.
The difference from test-and-set is the conditional store. It lets a thread say `only if nobody has touched this since I read it`, which is what makes retry possible.

If another thread got in between the read and the swap, the returned value differs from `old`, the loop goes round and the update is recomputed from the current value. Nothing is lost, but nothing is bounded either.

checkpoint.prompt: A test-and-set spin lock starts with `flag` at 0. The schedule is: T1 calls TestAndSet(&flag, 1); T2 calls TestAndSet(&flag, 1); T2 calls TestAndSet(&flag, 1) again; T1 calls unlock(); T2 calls TestAndSet(&flag, 1). For each call give the returned value and the value of `flag` afterwards, written as `returned, flag` - for example `1, 1`. For the unlock, give just the value of `flag`.
checkpoint.explain: A spinning thread's calls are not no-ops - each one really does write 1 - but since the flag was already 1 the write changes nothing, which is exactly why spinning is safe. The whole acquisition rests on the single call that returns 0: only one call can observe a free flag, so only one thread can believe it holds the lock. The tempting error is to expect a spinning call to return 0 because the caller is waiting; the return value describes the flag before the write, not the caller's intent.

guided-practice.prompt: `total` starts at 20. Two threads each perform one `total = total + 1`, decomposed into LOAD, ADD, STORE. The schedule is: T1 LOAD, T2 LOAD, T2 ADD, T2 STORE, T1 ADD, T1 STORE. Give the value held in memory by `total` after each instruction.
guided-practice.hint: Only a STORE changes memory. A thread's ADD works on the value it loaded, however long ago that was.
guided-practice.explain: T1 was preempted after its LOAD, so it is holding a 20 in a register while the world moves on without it. When it finally runs its ADD it computes 21 from that stale 20 - not from the 21 now in memory - and its STORE writes 21 over a 21. Both increments completed and the total rose by one. The common slip is to give 22 for the final step, on the assumption that T1's ADD re-reads memory; it does not, because the LOAD already happened.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete the vocabulary of mutual exclusion with the term each description names.
guided-practice.template:
the region of code that must not be interleaved: ___ section
the guarantee that at most one thread is inside it: ___ exclusion
the property of appearing to happen as one indivisible step: ___
an outcome that depends on the scheduler's choices: a ___ condition
the hardware instruction that returns the old value and writes a new one: ___
guided-practice.hint: All five are named in this floor's lesson, in the order the ideas were introduced.
guided-practice.explain: The distinction worth holding on to is between the critical section, which is a piece of your code, and mutual exclusion, which is a property enforced over it. Atomicity is what the pair buys you: the section is not really indivisible, it merely cannot be observed part-done. Test-and-set is the hardware's contribution, and it is a single instruction precisely because a two-instruction test-then-set would need a lock of its own.

guided-practice.prompt: Put the events of one successful acquisition of a test-and-set spin lock into the order they happen, for a thread that arrives while the lock is already held.
fragments: the thread calls TestAndSet(&flag, 1) and gets 1 back
seeing 1, it loops and calls TestAndSet again, still getting 1
the holder finishes its critical section and calls unlock, storing 0 into flag
the thread's next TestAndSet returns 0, having written 1
the thread leaves the spin loop and enters the critical section
guided-practice.hint: The step that releases the waiter is performed by the other thread, not by the waiter.
guided-practice.explain: The acquisition is the single call that returns 0, and it both tests and takes the lock in one indivisible action - there is no moment between them for another thread to slip in. Everything before it is wasted processor time, which is the spin lock's whole character: it converts waiting into burning cycles. Note that nothing here guarantees this thread is the one that succeeds after the unlock; a newly arriving thread may take it first, and that is exactly the unfairness a spin lock does not fix.

guided-practice.prompt: Two threads each execute `counter = counter + 1` exactly 1000 times, with no synchronisation at all, on a counter starting at 0. Give the number of increments issued, and the highest and lowest final values that some schedule can produce.
guided-practice.template:
increments issued in total: ___
highest possible final value: ___
lowest possible final value: ___
guided-practice.hint: The final value is always one more than something a thread loaded. Ask how small that loaded value can be made, given that the load must happen late.
guided-practice.explain: The highest is the answer you wanted, and it needs only that no thread is ever preempted between a load and its store. The lowest is 2, not 1000 and not 1: the last store to land writes one more than whatever its thread loaded, so to finish at 2 one thread must still be holding a stale 1 when everything else has run. Every value from 2 to 2000 is reachable by some schedule, which is the real lesson - an unsynchronised counter does not merely undercount by a predictable margin, it carries no information about how much work was done.

interleaving-lab.prompt: A shared `balance` starts at 100. Three threads A, B and C each run one `balance = balance + 1` as LOAD, ADD, STORE. The schedule is: A LOAD, A ADD, B LOAD, B ADD, B STORE, C LOAD, C ADD, C STORE, A STORE. Give the value in memory after each of the nine instructions.
interleaving-lab.hint: A has been holding a register since the very first instruction. Ask what is in it when A is finally allowed to store.
interleaving-lab.explain: The last step is the one that matters and the one most people get wrong: the balance goes **down**, from 102 to 101, because A stores the 101 it computed from a value it read eight instructions ago. Three increments were issued and the balance rose by one, so two updates were lost - B's is lost as well, silently overwritten by C's identical arithmetic. This is why a race is worse than an off-by-one: a stale store can move shared state backwards, and nothing in the data afterwards records that it happened.

interleaving-lab.prompt: An account `balance` starts at 200. Thread A runs a deposit (LOAD, ADD 50, STORE) and thread B runs a withdrawal (LOAD, SUBTRACT 30, STORE), with no lock. The schedule is: A LOAD, A ADD, B LOAD, B SUBTRACT, B STORE, A STORE. Give the value of `balance` in memory after each instruction, then the value it should have held.

steps.label: the correct balance after both operations

interleaving-lab.hint: Each thread writes back a value derived from what it read, not from what is there now.
interleaving-lab.explain: The withdrawal vanishes completely: A's store of 250 overwrites B's 170 with a figure computed before the withdrawal existed, and the customer is 30 better off than the ledger says. Reverse the last two instructions and the deposit vanishes instead - the same code, the same inputs, a different answer, which is the definition of a race. Note that no arithmetic is wrong anywhere; the fault is entirely that a read-modify-write was allowed to be observed part-done, which is precisely what a critical section around each operation would forbid.

interleaving-lab.prompt: A logging library keeps a shared `messages_written` count and appends to a shared buffer with no lock. It has run correctly for two years on single-core embedded hardware and passes its full test suite on the new eight-core board. In production on the new board the count drifts low - a few per million - and once a day a log line appears with two messages interleaved character by character. Name the cause and explain why the platform change exposed it.
interleaving-lab.answer: an existing data race, previously hidden because a single core made the interleaving window rare and never truly concurrent
interleaving-lab.hint: The code did not change. Ask what a second core allows that a single core, with the same threads, never did.
interleaving-lab.explain: The bug was always there; the hardware merely stopped hiding it. On one core two threads interleave only when the timer interrupt lands in the few-nanosecond window between a load and its store, so the race fires rarely enough to look like correctness. On eight cores the threads run genuinely simultaneously, so overlapping the critical region needs no interrupt at all and the window is hit constantly - hence a low but steady drift, and occasionally two appends running through the buffer at once. The tempting misdiagnosis is a compiler or toolchain fault, because 'it worked before the port' points that way, but a compiler bug would not produce a rate that scales with load, and a passing test suite proves nothing here: it shows only that these particular runs missed the window.

interleaving-lab.prompt: Two threads run `atomic_increment` on a shared `v` holding 7, using the loop `do { old = *v; } while (CompareAndSwap(v, old, old + 1) != old);`. The schedule is: A reads `old`; B reads `old`; B calls CompareAndSwap; A calls CompareAndSwap; A re-reads `old`; A calls CompareAndSwap again. For each read give the thread's `old` and then `v`; for each CompareAndSwap give its return value and then `v`. Write each answer as two numbers separated by a comma.

steps.label: final value of v after both increments

interleaving-lab.hint: CompareAndSwap always returns what it found. It writes only when what it found equals what was expected.
interleaving-lab.explain: A's first CompareAndSwap is the whole point: it returns 8 rather than 7, which is not equal to A's `old`, so it writes nothing and the loop goes round. That returned 8 is the difference between compare-and-swap and test-and-set - it reports the current value, so the retry recomputes the increment from fresh data and no update is lost. The result is 9, the correct answer, without a lock anywhere; the price is that A did the work twice, and under heavy contention a thread can retry many times, so lock-free is not the same thing as wait-free or even fast.

interleaving-lab.prompt: A developer argues that `counter++` must be safe because it is a single expression. Explain why the argument fails, what the processor actually executes, and why a `volatile` qualifier would not fix it either.
interleaving-lab.hint: Count the instructions the expression compiles to, then ask what `volatile` actually promises the compiler.
interleaving-lab.explain: Source syntax has no relationship to instruction boundaries: `counter++` compiles to a load into a register, an arithmetic operation on that register, and a store back, and the thread may be preempted - or simply run beside another core - in either gap, so a second thread can load the same stale value. `volatile` is the classic false fix because it sounds like it means 'shared'. It only forbids the compiler from caching the value in a register across statements and from reordering the accesses it governs; it still emits a load, an arithmetic operation and a store, so the read-modify-write remains three separately observable steps. What is needed is either a lock around the section or a genuinely atomic read-modify-write instruction, because atomicity is a property of the hardware operation, not of how briefly the source describes it.

lock-design.prompt: A team must protect a short critical section inside a device driver that also runs on a four-core machine. One engineer proposes masking interrupts around it; another proposes a test-and-set spin lock. Assess both. Say where each is correct and where each is not, what a spin lock costs on a single core versus on four, and what the two mechanisms together are actually used for in a driver.
lock-design.hint: Ask what each mechanism excludes. One excludes the interrupt handler on this core; the other excludes threads on other cores. A driver usually needs both.
lock-design.explain: The two mechanisms exclude different things, which is why the choice is not either/or. Masking interrupts stops the handler on **this** core from re-entering the section but says nothing about the other three cores, so alone it is not mutual exclusion on this machine. A spin lock excludes the threads on other cores but does not stop this core's own interrupt handler, which - if it takes the same lock while a thread on this core holds it - deadlocks the core instantly against itself. Real drivers therefore take both: mask locally, then spin. On the cost side, spinning is only ever reasonable when the section is short and there is somewhere else for the holder to run: on four cores a spinner burns a few hundred cycles while the holder finishes on another core, but on one core it burns its entire remaining quantum waiting for a holder that cannot possibly run until the spinner is preempted. The tempting simplification is 'spin locks are always wasteful'; the honest answer is that they are wasteful exactly when the holder is not running.

lock-design.prompt: A shared hash table is protected by one global lock. Each operation costs 10,000 ns in total, of which exactly 250 ns is spent inside the critical section. Assume the cores are identical and otherwise idle, and that keys are spread evenly over buckets. Give each figure as a plain number with no units and no thousands separators.

steps.label: operations per second one core can perform
serial fraction of one operation, as a percentage
greatest speedup any number of cores can achieve with the global lock
operations per second the single global lock can sustain, whatever the core count
number of cores at which the global lock becomes the bottleneck
operations per second sustainable with 16 independent per-bucket locks

lock-design.hint: A lock held for 250 ns can be handed on at most 1,000,000,000 / 250 times a second, and that number does not change when you buy more cores.
lock-design.explain: Two independent calculations meet at the same answer, which is the point. From the throughput side, a 250 ns critical section can be entered at most 4,000,000 times a second, and a core producing one operation per 10,000 ns manages 100,000 a second, so the fortieth core is the one that saturates the lock. From Amdahl's side, 250 of 10,000 ns is a 2.5 per cent serial fraction, and the ceiling on speedup is $1/0.025 = 40$ - the same 40. Splitting into 16 independent bucket locks multiplies the lock ceiling by 16 to 64,000,000, because sixteen critical sections can now be occupied at once. The tempting error is to expect fine-grained locking to raise the single-core figure; it does not, and in fact lowers it slightly through extra acquisitions - it only raises the ceiling.

lock-design.prompt: An in-memory cache uses one mutex around a hash table. On four cores it serves 380,000 requests a second. Moved to 32 cores it serves 340,000 - fewer than before - while every core shows high system time and the profiler attributes most of it to the lock acquisition path. Each request spends about 1 per cent of its time in the critical section. Name the cause and explain both why throughput stopped rising and why it fell.
lock-design.answer: contention on a single coarse-grained lock, whose serialised critical section caps throughput while the cost of contending grows with the core count
lock-design.hint: Work out the ceiling implied by a 1 per cent critical section, then ask what 32 cores do to each other while queueing for one word of memory.
lock-design.explain: A 1 per cent serial fraction caps speedup at 100 regardless of cores, so throughput was always going to flatten - but flattening does not explain a fall, and the fall is the real finding. Beyond a certain point the cost of contending exceeds the work being protected: every core attempting the atomic acquisition drags the lock's cache line to itself, so the line bounces between 32 caches and each acquisition costs far more than it did with four contenders, while the holder itself is slowed by the traffic. That is why system time rises and the profiler points at the acquisition path rather than at the table. The cure is granularity - shard the table so that independent keys take independent locks - and the tempting wrong cure is a faster lock implementation, which lowers the constant but leaves the single serialised region, and therefore the ceiling, exactly where it was.

lock-design.prompt: Design a shared counter for a server on 32 cores that is incremented millions of times a second and read - exactly, not approximately - roughly once a second. Set out the data layout, how an increment proceeds, how an exact read is obtained, and which atomic primitive each step needs. Justify your choice of granularity against a single mutex and against a single compare-and-swap loop, and state honestly what your design costs and where it could still go wrong. No code is required; the description must be precise enough to implement.
lock-design.explain: The shape the workload asks for is one counter per core - an array of 32 sub-counters, each padded to its own cache line - with an increment doing an atomic add to the entry for the core it is running on, and a read summing all 32. That trade is explicit: writes become almost uncontended, since each core touches a line no other core wants, while reads become 32 times more expensive and are the rare operation. A single mutex or a single compare-and-swap loop both concentrate every increment on one word, so the cache line holding it bounces between all 32 cores and throughput collapses under exactly the load described; the compare-and-swap loop is worse than it looks, because failure means retrying, so contention causes more traffic rather than less. The padding is not an optimisation but the point - without it several sub-counters share a cache line and the contention returns in a form invisible in the source, which is false sharing. The honest costs are memory, the cost of finding the current core's index, and the fact that summing without stopping the writers yields a total that was never simultaneously true of all shards. If 'exact' means a consistent snapshot rather than a correct sum of completed increments, the shards must be locked or a sequence-number scheme used, and that must be said rather than glossed over.

lock-design.prompt: State the three properties by which any lock implementation is judged, and for the test-and-set spin lock say how it fares on each. Then explain why a thread must never be descheduled and forgotten inside a critical section, and what that implies about how long a critical section ought to be.
lock-design.hint: Correctness, fairness, performance - and the spin lock scores very differently on each of the three.
lock-design.explain: Correctness, fairness and performance, and the spin lock's honest scorecard is: correct, unfair, and fast or catastrophic depending on the core count. It is correct because only one test-and-set can observe a free flag. It is unfair because a waiter holds no queue position, so an arriving thread may take the lock ahead of one that has spun for a million cycles and may keep doing so indefinitely - that is starvation, and it is what ticket locks exist to fix. Its performance is excellent uncontended, acceptable when contended across cores with a short section, and disastrous on a single core, where each spinner burns a whole quantum waiting for a holder that cannot run. That last case is the general rule in miniature: while a thread sits inside a critical section, every other thread wanting that data makes no progress, so the holder being preempted converts one thread's pause into everyone's. Hence critical sections should hold only what genuinely must be indivisible - never blocking I/O, never work that could have been done before the lock was taken.

exam.prompt: Which definition of a **critical section** is correct?
choices: any region of code that accesses a shared resource and must not be executed by more than one thread at a time
the part of the kernel that runs with interrupts disabled
a thread's private stack, which no other thread may read
the portion of a program that dominates its running time
exam.explain: A critical section is defined by the invariant it maintains over shared data, not by where it sits or how long it runs. The interrupt-disabled answer confuses a section with one particular way of protecting one, and only on a uniprocessor at that. The stack is the one part of a thread that needs no protection, since nobody else touches it, and the last choice describes the hot path - a performance notion with no bearing on correctness.

exam.prompt: Select every item that all threads of one process share.
choices: the code (text) segment
global variables
the heap
the stack
the register set and program counter
the page table
exam.explain: Threads share the address space, so everything that **is** the address space - code, globals, heap, and the page table that describes them - is common, which is exactly why a switch between threads of one process need not flush the TLB. The stack and the register state are private because they record where a particular thread is in its own execution. The page table is the one people hesitate over, but it must be shared: if the threads had different page tables they would not have the same address space, and they would be processes.

exam.prompt: Fill in each blank with a single term from this floor.
exam.template:
A read-modify-write that another thread can observe part-done lacks ___.
The instruction that writes only if the word still holds an expected value is ___.
A lock that waits by looping rather than sleeping is a ___ lock.
Protecting more data with one lock is called ___ granularity.
exam.explain: Compare-and-swap is the conditional one - test-and-set writes unconditionally and merely tells you what was there - and that conditionality is what makes retry loops possible. Coarse granularity trades throughput for the ease of getting it right; fine granularity does the reverse and introduces the possibility of two threads taking two locks in two different orders.

exam.prompt: `counter` starts at 4. Thread T1 performs two increments and thread T2 performs one, each as LOAD, ADD, STORE. The schedule is: T1 LOAD, T1 ADD, T1 STORE, T2 LOAD, T2 ADD, T1 LOAD, T1 ADD, T1 STORE, T2 STORE. Give the value in memory after each instruction, then the value it should have held.
exam.explain: T1's first increment is untouched by anyone and lands cleanly, which is why races are so easy to miss: most of the work is fine. The loss happens because T2 loads 5 and is then held off while T1 loads the same 5 and stores 6; T2's store of its own 6 overwrites T1's with the identical number. Three increments were issued and the counter moved by two. The tempting answer for the ninth step is 7, on the assumption that T2's store adds to whatever is there - it does not, it writes the register.

exam.prompt: A test-and-set spin lock has `flag` at 1, held by T1. Give the returned value and the resulting flag, written as `returned, flag`, for each event: T2 spins once; T3 spins once; T1 unlocks (give the flag only); T3 spins again; T2 spins again.
exam.explain: T3 acquires and T2 keeps spinning, even though T2 arrived first - the trace is a small demonstration that a test-and-set lock has no queue and therefore no fairness guarantee at all. Each unsuccessful call still writes 1 over a 1, which is harmless, and that harmlessness is why the loop can be so simple. The one call that returns 0 is the acquisition; there is no separate 'take the lock' step, because there could not be one without reopening the race.

exam.prompt: The kernel of a new operating system protects all its internal data with a single pair of disable-interrupts and enable-interrupts calls, and the design worked on the prototype board. The product ships on a four-core processor and corrupts kernel structures under load. Explain what went wrong and what must replace the mechanism.
exam.explain: Masking interrupts prevents this core from being interrupted and nothing more. On the single-core prototype that was sufficient, because preventing preemption on the only core prevented every possible interleaving; on four cores the other three carry on executing kernel code, so two cores can be inside the same critical section simultaneously with no interrupt involved anywhere. The replacement must be built on a hardware atomic instruction - test-and-set or compare-and-swap - because only an operation that is indivisible across the whole memory system can exclude a thread on another core. In practice the local masking is kept as well, since it is still the only thing that excludes this core's own interrupt handler, so the fix is a lock plus masking rather than a lock instead of it. The tempting conclusion is that the prototype code was simply wrong; it was correct for the machine it was written for, which is why the assumption has to be found rather than merely the bug.

exam.prompt: A queue is protected by a mutex. A profiler shows that threads spend 40 per cent of their time waiting for it, and the critical section is found to contain the dequeue, a `write()` of the item to a log file on disk, and a call to `free()`. Throughput does not improve when the mutex is replaced with a faster spin lock; it gets worse. Name the cause and explain both observations.
exam.answer: the critical section is far too long because blocking I/O was placed inside it, so the lock is held across a disk write
exam.explain: The `write()` is the fault: a disk write takes on the order of milliseconds and the lock is held throughout, so every other thread waits on hardware it has no interest in, and the holder is descheduled while blocked - still holding the lock. The fix is to shorten the section, not to speed up the lock: dequeue under the mutex, then log and free outside it. The second observation is the confirmation, and it is why the spin lock made things worse rather than merely failing to help. A blocking mutex at least lets a waiter sleep and yield the core to someone useful, whereas a spin lock has each waiter burn its whole quantum looping on a flag whose holder is asleep on a disk request. Spinning is only ever right when the holder is running and will be finished in less time than a context switch costs, and a thread blocked on I/O is the exact opposite of that.

exam.prompt: You are reviewing a proposal to replace a bank ledger's single global mutex with one mutex per account, on the grounds that transfers between unrelated accounts should proceed in parallel. Argue for and against, and set out precisely what the transfer operation must now do that it did not have to do before.
exam.explain: The case for is straightforward and real: with one lock per account, transfers touching disjoint accounts contend for nothing, and the throughput ceiling rises from one transfer at a time to as many as there are cores. The case against is that a transfer is not an operation on one account. It must hold both accounts' locks for the whole of the debit and the credit, or another thread can observe the money in neither place; and once an operation takes two locks, two transfers running in opposite directions - A to B and B to A - can each take one and wait forever for the other. The discipline that fixes it is a global ordering: always acquire in a fixed order, such as ascending account identifier or address, so a cycle is impossible. The proposal must also say what happens to any operation that reads the whole ledger - an audit that sums the balances now has no single lock to take and must either take all of them in that same order or accept a total that was never simultaneously true. That is the real trade: fine granularity buys parallelism and charges for it in invariants that the programmer, rather than the lock, must now maintain.

sections.title: Waiting for a condition, not for a lock
sections.body:
A lock answers one question: may I touch this data now? It cannot answer the other question a concurrent program constantly asks - **has something happened yet?** A thread that must wait until a child has finished, until a buffer holds an item, until a disk request has completed, has nothing useful to do, and spinning on a shared flag burns a whole CPU to discover nothing.

A **condition variable** is an explicit queue of sleeping threads attached to a state change. `pthread_cond_wait(&c, &m)` puts the caller on that queue and, atomically with going to sleep, **releases the mutex** - then reacquires it before returning. `pthread_cond_signal(&c)` wakes one waiter. The atomic release is the whole trick: without it the waiter would either sleep holding the lock, so nobody could ever change the state it is waiting for, or release first and risk the change happening in the gap before it sleeps, leaving it asleep with nobody left to wake it.

Two rules follow, and neither is negotiable. **Always hold the lock when calling wait or signal**, because the state you are testing and the sleep must not be separated by a window in which another thread can act. **Always wait in a `while` loop, never an `if`**, because POSIX condition variables have Mesa semantics: a signal makes the waiter **runnable**, it does not hand it the CPU or the invariant. Between the signal and the waiter actually running, some third thread can acquire the mutex and undo the very condition that was signalled - so on waking, the only safe move is to test the predicate again.

The cost of a condition variable is that it holds no memory. Signalling when no one is waiting does nothing at all; the signal is not saved. That is why the shared state, never the signal, is the source of truth - and why `thr_join` below still works when the child finishes first.

annotations.text: The state changes **before** the signal, and both happen under the lock. Signalling first would wake a thread that then re-tests `done`, still sees 0, and sleeps again - possibly for ever, since the signal was not saved.
`while`, not `if`. Even in this two-thread case the loop costs nothing, and it is the only version that survives a third thread, a spurious wakeup, or a signal that another waiter consumed first.

`pthread_cond_wait` takes the mutex because it must release it while sleeping and reacquire it before returning. The line after it therefore runs with the lock held again, exactly as though the wait had never happened.

checkpoint.prompt: Complete the waiting half of the join, so that it is correct under Mesa semantics.
checkpoint.explain: `if` compiles and usually appears to work, which is what makes it dangerous: it is only wrong when a signalled thread is overtaken before it runs, which is rare, timing-dependent and impossible to reproduce on demand. Passing the mutex is not bookkeeping either - `wait` must release it atomically with sleeping, so a version that took no mutex could not exist without reintroducing the lost-wakeup race.

sections.title: The bounded buffer, done properly
sections.body:
Producer/consumer is the shape almost every real coordination problem takes: one side generates work, the other consumes it, and a fixed-size buffer between them decouples their speeds. The buffer being bounded is what creates **two** waiting conditions rather than one - consumers wait when it is empty, producers wait when it is full - and getting from a plausible solution to a correct one takes two separate corrections.

The first correction is the `while` loop, for the reason the previous section gave. With a single producer and a single consumer an `if` survives; add a second consumer and it fails, because the signalled consumer can be overtaken by another consumer that takes the item, so the first wakes to an empty buffer and reads rubbish.

The second correction is subtler and is why the code below has **two** condition variables. With one shared queue, a consumer's signal can wake another **consumer** instead of the producer. Suppose a one-slot buffer, one producer and two consumers: both consumers sleep on the empty buffer; the producer fills it, signals, wakes the first consumer, then loops round, finds the buffer full and sleeps; the woken consumer takes the item and signals - waking the second consumer rather than the producer; that consumer re-tests, finds the buffer empty and sleeps again. All three threads are now asleep with no one left to signal. The program is deadlocked, and nothing about it looks wrong.

Two condition variables fix this by construction: producers only ever sleep on `empty` and are only ever woken by consumers, consumers only ever sleep on `fill` and are only ever woken by producers. The rule generalises - **one condition variable per condition being waited for.** `pthread_cond_broadcast` is the blunt alternative, waking everyone so that whoever can proceed does; it is always correct and costs a stampede of threads that mostly re-test and go back to sleep.

annotations.text: Two queues, named for the condition a sleeper is waiting for. The `empty` queue holds producers waiting for a free slot; the `fill` queue holds consumers waiting for an item. Sharing one queue is what lets a consumer wake a consumer.

`count == MAX` is the producer's predicate and it is re-tested on every wakeup. Waking does not mean a slot is free - it means a slot **was** free at some point, which is a different and much weaker claim.
The producer signals `fill`, the queue only consumers sleep on, so this wakeup can never be wasted on another producer. That directedness is the entire benefit of the second condition variable.

checkpoint.prompt: A bounded buffer with `MAX = 3` starts empty and uses the code above. Give the value of `count` after each operation. If an operation must block, give the unchanged value of `count`.
checkpoint.explain: The last put finds `count == MAX`, so it waits on `empty` and changes nothing - the count stays at 3 until a consumer makes room. A blocked producer is not an error condition or a dropped item: back-pressure is the whole purpose of bounding the buffer, and it is what stops a fast producer from consuming unbounded memory.

sections.title: Semaphores: one primitive, two jobs
sections.body:
A **semaphore** is an integer with two atomic operations and a waiting queue. `sem_wait` decrements it and blocks the caller while the value is negative; `sem_post` increments it and wakes one waiter if any are queued. The initial value decides everything about what the semaphore is for, and the sign carries information: when the value is negative, its magnitude is exactly the number of threads waiting.

Initialised to 1, it is a **binary semaphore** - a lock. One thread's `sem_wait` takes the value to 0 and it proceeds; the next takes it to -1 and sleeps; the holder's `sem_post` returns it to 0 and releases one sleeper. Initialised to 0, the same primitive expresses **ordering**: a parent that calls `sem_wait` before the child has called `sem_post` goes to -1 and sleeps, and a child that posts first leaves the value at 1 so the parent's later wait succeeds immediately. Unlike a condition variable, a semaphore **remembers** - which is why an ordering semaphore needs no separate state variable and no `while` loop.

Initialised to N, it is a **counting semaphore** and its value is a count of available resources. The bounded buffer becomes three semaphores and no explicit predicate at all: `empty` starts at MAX, `full` at 0, and a binary `mutex` at 1.

The ordering of the two waits in `put` is not stylistic. Take the mutex first and then block on `empty` and you have gone to sleep holding the lock; the consumer that would free a slot cannot get the mutex, and both threads wait for ever. **The mutex must be the innermost acquisition** - the general rule being never to sleep on anything while holding a lock that the thread which would wake you also needs.

The **reader/writer** problem is the classic counting-semaphore application: many readers may share the data, but a writer needs it alone. The usual solution keeps a reader count under a small lock and has only the **first** reader acquire the write lock and only the **last** reader release it - so readers pay a lock acquisition each but do not exclude one another. Its well-known flaw is that a steady stream of readers never lets the count fall to zero, so a waiting writer starves indefinitely.

annotations.text: `full` starts at 0 because nothing has been produced. A consumer arriving first drives it to -1 and sleeps, and the magnitude of the negative value is the number of consumers queued.

`empty` is waited on **before** `mutex`. Reverse these two lines and a producer that finds the buffer full falls asleep holding the mutex, so no consumer can ever drain it - a two-line change that deadlocks the program.

`full` is posted after the mutex is released. Posting while still holding the lock is merely wasteful rather than wrong: the woken consumer would immediately block on a mutex the poster has not yet dropped.

checkpoint.prompt: A semaphore is initialised to 2. Four threads A, B, C and D operate on it in this order. Give the semaphore's value after each operation.
checkpoint.explain: The value never clamps at zero: it goes negative and the magnitude counts the sleepers, which is how `sem_post` knows there is somebody to wake. Reading the fourth step as 'back to 2 because A is done' is the tempting error - A's post is consumed by C, which was already queued, so the resource is handed straight on rather than returned to the free pool.

sections.title: Deadlock, and the one cure that is used in practice
sections.body:
Deadlock is a set of threads each holding something another needs, so none can proceed. Coffman showed it requires **four** conditions simultaneously, and breaking any one of them prevents it: **mutual exclusion** (a resource can be held exclusively), **hold-and-wait** (a thread holds one resource while requesting another), **no pre-emption** (a resource cannot be taken back by force), and **circular wait** (a cycle in the wait-for graph).

Each condition suggests a cure, and three of them are unattractive. Removing mutual exclusion means lock-free data structures built from atomic compare-and-swap - genuinely deadlock-free, and hard enough to get right that mostly only library authors attempt it. Removing hold-and-wait means acquiring every lock you will ever need at once under one global lock, which needs the whole set known in advance and destroys concurrency. Removing no pre-emption means `pthread_mutex_trylock` and releasing everything on failure - correct, but it introduces livelock, where threads repeatedly grab and back off in lockstep and make no progress, so it needs randomised delay to be practical.

**Avoidance** is the fourth option and belongs to textbooks rather than kernels: given advance knowledge of every thread's maximum resource demand, an algorithm such as Banker's schedules only into safe states. Real systems do not have that knowledge. **Detection** is the pragmatic cousin - build the wait-for graph periodically, look for a cycle, and recover by killing or restarting a victim. Databases do exactly this, because aborting a transaction is a cheap and already-supported operation; an operating system usually has no equivalent way to unwind a thread.

Which leaves **lock ordering**, and it is the answer nearly every real codebase uses. Define a total order over all locks and require every thread to acquire in that order; a cycle would need some thread to acquire out of order, so no cycle can form. When there is no natural order - two accounts, two nodes, two files of the same kind - use the addresses of the lock objects, which are arbitrary but consistent, and that is enough. The cost is discipline: the ordering is a global invariant that no single function can enforce on its own, and it is easy to break by calling out of a critical section into code that takes locks you cannot see.

annotations.text: `transfer(a, b)` and `transfer(b, a)` running concurrently acquire the two locks in opposite orders, and each can hold one while waiting for the other. That is circular wait, and the code is correct in every single-threaded test you can write.

Comparing the pointers imposes a total order that has no meaning but is consistent everywhere, which is all an ordering has to be. Every thread now takes the lower-addressed lock first, so no cycle can form.

This still deadlocks on `transfer(a, a)`, where `first` and `second` are the same lock and a non-recursive mutex blocks on itself. Self-transfer needs an explicit early return - a reminder that an ordering removes circular wait between distinct locks and nothing else.

checkpoint.prompt: Put the reasoning for adopting a lock ordering into the order in which it is actually made.
fragments: observe that two threads acquire the same pair of locks in different orders
note that this permits a cycle in the wait-for graph, which is Coffman's circular wait
define a total order over the locks - by role, or by address where there is no natural one
require every thread to acquire locks in that order, releasing in any order it likes
conclude that no cycle can form, because a cycle would need some thread to acquire out of order
checkpoint.explain: The argument runs from the observed hazard to the invariant that excludes it, and the last step is what makes lock ordering a proof rather than a habit: a cycle requires at least one thread to have acquired in decreasing order, so forbidding that forbids the cycle. Note the ordering constrains only acquisition - release order is free, which is why the discipline costs so little at runtime.

guided-practice.prompt: A parent uses `thr_join` and a child uses `thr_exit` from the lesson, with `done` starting at 0. The child runs to completion **before** the parent ever calls `thr_join`. Give the value of `done` after each event, and for the final step answer yes or no.

steps.label: parent locks m and tests the predicate

guided-practice.explain: The signal went to an empty queue and was discarded - condition variables keep no memory of it - yet the join still works, because the parent consults `done` rather than the signal. This is why the shared state is the source of truth: a version that slept unconditionally and waited for a signal would hang for ever here, and would appear to work only when the child happened to be slow.

guided-practice.prompt: Complete the consumer so that it sleeps on the right queue, re-tests its own predicate, and wakes the right thread.
guided-practice.explain: A consumer waits for an item, so it sleeps on `fill`, and it signals `empty` to tell a producer a slot has opened. Sleeping and signalling on the same variable is the classic error: it lets a consumer's signal wake another consumer, and with two consumers that is exactly the interleaving that puts every thread to sleep at once.

guided-practice.prompt: A mutex is built from a semaphore initialised to 1. Threads A, B and C use it in this order. Give the semaphore's value after each operation.
guided-practice.explain: Only A is in the critical section; the value of -2 says two threads are queued behind it, and each post hands the lock straight to a sleeper rather than returning the value to 1. The value reaches 1 again only when the last holder leaves with nobody waiting, which is exactly the definition of an unheld lock.

guided-practice.prompt: Put the body of `rwlock_acquire_readlock` into the order in which it must run.
fragments: sem_wait(&rw->lock) - take the small lock guarding the reader count
rw->readers++
if (rw->readers == 1) sem_wait(&rw->writelock) - the first reader excludes writers
sem_post(&rw->lock) - release the small lock so other readers can enter
guided-practice.explain: The counter must be incremented and tested under its own lock, or two readers arriving together could both see themselves as the first and both try to take the write lock. Only the transition from zero to one readers touches `writelock`, which is what lets readers share: the second and later readers pay one quick lock acquisition and nothing more.

guided-practice.prompt: A reader/writer lock as in the previous question. Events arrive in this order: R1 acquires a read lock, R2 acquires a read lock, W requests the write lock, R3 acquires a read lock. Give the reader count after each event, then say whether W is running or blocked.

steps.label: after W requests the write lock

guided-practice.explain: R3 arrives after W and sails past it, because `writelock` is already held by R1 on behalf of all readers and R3, not being the first reader, never touches `writelock` at all. The waiting writer is invisible to arriving readers, and while readers keep overlapping the count never reaches zero - this is reader starvation, and it is a property of the design rather than of bad luck.

synchronisation-lab.prompt: A bounded buffer with one producer and two consumers uses `if (count == 0) pthread_cond_wait(&fill, &m);` instead of a `while`. It runs correctly for hours, then a consumer returns a stale value from an empty buffer. Name the underlying cause and give the interleaving that produces it.
synchronisation-lab.answer: Mesa semantics: the signalled consumer is only made runnable, and the other consumer takes the item before it runs, so the predicate is false again by the time it returns from wait
synchronisation-lab.explain: Under Mesa semantics a signal is a hint that the condition held at some past moment, not a handover of the invariant. The producer signals, consumer one becomes runnable but does not run; consumer two acquires the mutex first, consumes the only item and leaves `count` at 0; consumer one then returns from `wait`, and with an `if` there is no second test, so it reads a slot that holds nothing. The `while` costs one extra comparison in the common case and is the only version that is correct. The tempting misdiagnosis is a missing lock or a memory-visibility problem - but the mutex is held correctly throughout, and it is the staleness of the signal, not the visibility of the data, that breaks.

synchronisation-lab.prompt: A one-slot bounded buffer uses a single condition variable `cond` for both waiting conditions, with correct `while` loops and correct locking everywhere. With one producer and two consumers it eventually stops dead with all three threads asleep. Name the cause, give the interleaving, and name the two fixes.
synchronisation-lab.answer: One condition variable shared by both roles lets a consumer's signal wake another consumer instead of the producer, so the only thread that could make progress is never woken
synchronisation-lab.explain: Both consumers sleep on the empty buffer. The producer fills it, signals, wakes consumer one, then loops, finds the buffer full and sleeps on the same queue behind consumer two. Consumer one takes the item and signals - and the queue head is consumer two, not the producer, so a consumer is woken; it re-tests, finds the buffer empty and sleeps again, as does consumer one. All three now sleep and no signal will ever come. The fix is one condition variable per condition, so producers are only woken by consumers and consumers only by producers; `pthread_cond_broadcast` also works, by waking everyone at the cost of a stampede of threads that mostly go straight back to sleep. Note that the `while` loops are not the bug here - they are correct, and they are what makes the failure a silent deadlock rather than corrupted data.

synchronisation-lab.prompt: The semaphore bounded buffer from the lesson, with `MAX = 3`, `empty` at 3 and `full` at 0. Four producers each call `put` once, then one consumer calls `get`. Give the pair `empty,full` - written exactly like `2,1` - after each producer's `put` completes or blocks, then after the consumer's `get`, then after the blocked producer resumes and finishes its `put`.

steps.label: P4 calls put and blocks on empty
after P4 resumes and finishes its put

synchronisation-lab.explain: `empty` and `full` are not two views of one counter that must always sum to MAX - they are one resource count each, and while a producer is queued their sum is 2 rather than 3, because that producer has already claimed a slot it has not yet filled. The consumer's `sem_post(&empty)` takes the value from -1 to 0 and hands the slot directly to P4, which is why P4's completion adds to `full` without decrementing `empty` again: it did that before it slept. Expecting `empty` to stop at 0 is the usual error, and it loses exactly the information `sem_post` needs in order to know somebody is waiting.

synchronisation-lab.prompt: A cache in a web server is guarded by the reader/writer lock from the lesson. Under load the read rate never drops to zero and the invalidation thread, which needs the write lock, has not run in forty minutes - stale entries are being served. Explain why the lock's own design causes this, and describe a change that lets the writer through without abandoning shared reading.
synchronisation-lab.explain: The write lock is released only when the reader count falls to zero, and an arriving reader that is not the first never consults `writelock` at all - so a waiting writer is invisible to new readers, and overlapping reads keep the count permanently above zero. The standard repair makes arriving readers pass through a turnstile semaphore that a waiting writer holds: readers already inside finish and drain the count normally, but new readers queue behind the writer, so the count reaches zero in bounded time. Shared reading is untouched in the common case, since the turnstile is uncontended when no writer is waiting. The tempting non-fix is to make the writer retry more aggressively or to raise its priority - neither helps, because the writer is not losing a race, it is waiting on a condition that arriving readers actively prevent from ever occurring.

synchronisation-lab.prompt: A parent thread must not proceed until its child has finished. A colleague proposes a semaphore initialised to 0, with the child calling `sem_post` and the parent `sem_wait`, and objects that this cannot be right because it has no `while` loop and no shared state variable. Explain why the semaphore version is correct in both orderings, and what a condition variable would need in its place.
synchronisation-lab.explain: A semaphore carries state - its value - so a `sem_post` that arrives before anyone waits is not lost: it leaves the value at 1 and the parent's later `sem_wait` succeeds immediately. Parent first drives the value to -1 and sleeps until the child's post wakes it. Both orderings work, and no predicate is needed because the count is the predicate. A condition variable is stateless by comparison: a signal delivered to an empty queue is discarded, so the same handshake needs an explicit `done` flag, the mutex that guards it, and a `while` loop testing it - which is precisely the `thr_join` from the lesson. The colleague's instinct is right in general and wrong here: the `while` loop exists to re-test a predicate that another thread can falsify, and the semaphore initialised to zero has no such predicate to falsify.

deadlock-clinic.prompt: Three threads and three mutexes. T1 takes A then B, T2 takes B then C, T3 takes C then A. They interleave in this order: T1 takes A, T2 takes B, T3 takes C, T1 requests B, T2 requests C, T3 requests A. For each of the last three requests answer `blocks` or `proceeds`, then give the number of threads in the wait-for cycle.

steps.label: how many threads are in the wait-for cycle?

deadlock-clinic.explain: The wait-for graph is T1 to T2 to T3 back to T1 - a cycle of three - and every thread holds one lock while requesting another, so all four Coffman conditions hold at once. Deadlock is not confined to pairs, which is why the two-thread mental picture misleads: a detector must look for a cycle of any length, and a codebase can satisfy 'never take these two locks in the wrong order' for every pair while still forming a three-way cycle.

deadlock-clinic.prompt: A banking service runs `transfer(from, to, amount)` exactly as written in the lesson's first function. It has passed every test, including a stress test with a thousand threads all transferring from account A to account B. In production it hangs within a day. Name the cause, and say why the stress test could never have found it.
deadlock-clinic.answer: Circular wait from inconsistent lock ordering: transfer(a,b) and transfer(b,a) running concurrently each hold one account lock and request the other
deadlock-clinic.explain: The function locks `from` then `to`, so the acquisition order depends on the arguments rather than on any global rule. Two concurrent calls in opposite directions each take one lock and wait for the other, closing a two-thread cycle. The stress test drove enormous concurrency but only ever in one direction, so every thread acquired A then B - a consistent order, and therefore no cycle possible. This is the characteristic shape of a deadlock bug: the hazard is a property of the combination of call sites, so no amount of load on a single call pattern exposes it, and the fix is a global invariant, such as ordering by lock address, that no individual function can establish alone.

deadlock-clinic.prompt: You maintain a graph store where an edge operation must lock two nodes, and node objects have no natural ordering. Propose a deadlock-free acquisition scheme, justify why it removes circular wait, name the case your scheme must special-case, and say what you would do instead if node locks had to be acquired one at a time as a traversal discovers them.
deadlock-clinic.explain: With no natural order, any consistent one will do: compare the lock addresses or stable node identifiers and always take the lower first. That removes circular wait because a cycle needs some thread to have acquired in decreasing order. The case to special-case is a self-edge, where both nodes are the same node and a non-recursive mutex would block on itself - test for equality and take the lock once. A traversal that discovers nodes as it goes cannot pre-sort them, so ordering does not apply; there the tool is `trylock`, releasing everything already held on failure and retrying, which attacks no pre-emption instead. That trade is worth naming: it swaps a deadlock for a possible livelock, so the retry needs randomised backoff, and it costs repeated work every time an attempt is abandoned.

deadlock-clinic.prompt: For each of the four Coffman conditions, name a technique that removes it, then explain why lock ordering dominates in practice while avoidance is essentially absent from real systems.
deadlock-clinic.explain: Mutual exclusion is removed by lock-free structures built on compare-and-swap - correct, and hard enough that it is left to library authors. Hold-and-wait is removed by acquiring the whole lock set atomically under a global lock, which needs the set known in advance and serialises everything. No pre-emption is removed by `trylock` with release-and-retry, which trades deadlock for livelock and needs randomised backoff. Circular wait is removed by a total order on locks, and it wins because it costs nothing at runtime, needs no advance knowledge, and leaves concurrency untouched - it is purely a discipline on the order of acquisition. Avoidance in the Banker's-algorithm sense requires every thread's maximum future demand up front and a scheduler willing to refuse safe-looking requests; general-purpose systems have neither, which is why detection with a victim, as databases do by aborting a transaction, is the only dynamic scheme that sees real use.

exam.prompt: Under Mesa semantics, what does `pthread_cond_signal` guarantee to the woken thread?
choices: That it becomes runnable and will reacquire the mutex before returning from `wait`, and nothing more
That the condition it was waiting for is true when it resumes
That it runs immediately, before the signalling thread continues
That no other thread can acquire the mutex until it has finished
exam.explain: Choice two describes Hoare semantics, in which the signaller hands over the lock and the invariant directly; almost no real system implements it, because it forces an immediate context switch. Under Mesa the signal is a hint about the past, so between the signal and the waiter running, another thread may acquire the mutex and falsify the condition - which is precisely why the predicate must be re-tested in a `while` loop.

exam.prompt: Which of these are Coffman conditions for deadlock? Select all that apply.
choices: Mutual exclusion - a resource can be held exclusively
Hold-and-wait - a thread holds one resource while requesting another
No pre-emption - a held resource cannot be taken back by force
Circular wait - a cycle exists in the wait-for graph
Priority inversion - a low-priority thread holds a lock a high-priority thread needs
exam.explain: The four are jointly necessary, so breaking any one prevents deadlock entirely - which is why the list is a menu of cures rather than a taxonomy. Priority inversion is a real and serious scheduling pathology, but the threads involved all eventually run: it delays progress rather than making it impossible, so it is not deadlock.

exam.prompt: Complete `put` for the semaphore bounded buffer so that it neither corrupts the buffer nor sleeps holding the lock.
exam.explain: A producer consumes a free slot and produces an item, so it waits on `empty` and posts `full`. The order matters as much as the names: with `mutex` taken first, a producer that finds the buffer full sleeps while holding the lock the consumer needs in order to drain it, and both threads then wait for ever.

exam.prompt: A semaphore is initialised to 1. Give its value after each of these operations, performed in order by distinct threads: wait, wait, wait, post, post.
exam.explain: The negative magnitude is the number of threads asleep on the semaphore, which is how `sem_post` knows whether it must wake anyone. A trace that floors the value at 0 loses that count, and an implementation that did so would leave woken threads permanently queued.

exam.prompt: Put the events of the classic one-condition-variable deadlock into the order in which they occur. The buffer holds one slot; there is one producer and two consumers, all with correct `while` loops.
fragments: both consumers find the buffer empty and sleep on the single condition variable
the producer fills the slot, signals, and wakes the first consumer
the producer loops round, finds the buffer full, and sleeps behind the second consumer
the first consumer takes the item and signals, waking the second consumer rather than the producer
the second consumer re-tests, finds the buffer empty and sleeps again, leaving every thread asleep
exam.explain: The fatal step is the fourth: a signal from a consumer lands on a queue that contains consumers, so the one thread able to make progress is never woken. Two condition variables make the wakeup directed - producers sleep only on `empty`, consumers only on `fill` - and `broadcast` fixes it by brute force, waking everyone so that whoever can proceed does.

exam.prompt: A reader/writer lock. R1 and R2 hold read locks, a writer W is blocked, and the readers now release. Give the reader count after each release, then say which release frees the write lock.

steps.label: which release frees the write lock? (R1/R2)

exam.explain: Only the last reader out posts `writelock`, mirroring the rule that only the first reader in takes it. R1's release changes nothing for the writer, which is why a stream of overlapping readers can keep the count above zero indefinitely and starve W - the writer waits not for any particular reader but for the count to reach zero.

exam.prompt: In a semaphore bounded buffer someone has swapped the first two lines of `put`, so that it reads `sem_wait(&mutex); sem_wait(&empty);`. Once the buffer fills, the whole program stops. Name the cause and explain why no consumer can rescue it.
exam.answer: The producer sleeps on empty while holding the mutex, and the consumer needs that same mutex to remove an item, so neither can proceed
exam.explain: The producer blocks on `empty` while still holding `mutex`. The only thread that can make `empty` positive is a consumer, and the consumer's first act after `sem_wait(&full)` is to take `mutex` - which the sleeping producer holds. Each waits for the other, and the general rule the swap violates is that the mutex must be the innermost acquisition: never sleep on a condition while holding a lock needed by the thread that would signal it. Blaming the buffer size or the initial value of `empty` is the tempting misreading, but the same two lines deadlock at any capacity as soon as the buffer fills.

exam.prompt: Explain why a thread must hold the mutex when it calls `pthread_cond_wait`, and why the call releases that mutex itself rather than expecting the caller to unlock first.
exam.explain: The predicate is shared state, so testing it requires the lock; and the test and the decision to sleep must be a single indivisible act. Unlocking first would open a window in which another thread changes the state and signals before the caller is on the queue - the lost wakeup, after which the caller sleeps for ever with the condition already true. Sleeping while holding the lock is no better: nobody could then acquire it to change the state or to signal. Only releasing atomically with going to sleep avoids both, and `wait` reacquires the mutex before returning so that the code after it can re-test the predicate safely.

sections.title: How the CPU talks to a device
sections.body:
A device is not a magic peripheral; it is a small pile of registers the CPU can read and write, and a protocol saying in what order. Almost every device exposes the same three: a **status** register saying whether it is busy, a **command** register saying what to do, and a **data** register carrying the operand. The canonical driver therefore does four things - wait until not busy, write the parameters, issue the command, wait until not busy again - and the whole of the I/O stack exists to hide those four steps behind `read()`.

The two waits are the problem. **Polling** means spinning on the status register, which burns a processor for the whole of a millisecond-scale disk operation while a runnable process sits in the ready queue. **Interrupts** let the driver block the caller and hand the CPU to somebody else; the device raises a line when it finishes, the CPU traps, and the handler wakes the sleeper. Interrupts are not free, though - the trap, the handler and the two context switches cost single-digit microseconds - so for a device that finishes faster than that overhead, polling is genuinely the cheaper choice, and at very high completion rates interrupts can **livelock** the machine, which is why fast NICs and NVMe drives coalesce interrupts or poll under load.

Even with interrupts, step 3a is still theft: `outsl` makes the CPU copy the block a word at a time, so moving 4 KB costs about a thousand loads and stores, and moving 1 GB costs roughly a quarter of a second of pure copying. **Direct memory access** replaces it with a separate engine: the CPU tells the DMA controller an address and a length, the controller moves the bytes across the bus on its own, and it raises the interrupt when the transfer is done. The CPU's involvement drops from **proportional to the data** to **constant per request**, which is what makes a modern device's bandwidth reachable at all.

annotations.text: The first wait is pure overhead - the CPU is spinning to learn something it could be told. Replacing it with sleep-until-interrupt is what lets another process run during the wait.

Parameters go into the data-side registers **before** the command that consumes them. The protocol is ordered, and a driver that issues the command first operates on whatever the last request left behind.
Programmed I/O: this single line is BSIZE/4 = 1024 word transfers executed by the processor for one 4 KB block. DMA deletes this line and pays one setup cost instead.
The second wait is the one worth an interrupt: on a disk it is the millisecond-scale one, whereas the first is usually short.

checkpoint.prompt: Put the four steps of the programmed-I/O protocol into the order a correct driver must perform them.
fragments: Poll the status register until the device reports it is no longer busy
